santhoshini.velusamy@uwaterloo.ca **Abstract** We study the one-pass streaming complexity of CSPs over a fixed finite relation _R_ under three natural objectives: SAT(_R_), deciding whether all constraints can be satisfied; Min-CSP(_R_), approximately minimizing the number of unsatisfied constraints; and Exact-CSP(_R_), exactly computing the maximum number of satisfied constraints. Sharma and Velusamy (ESA 2026) characterized the streaming complexity of satisfiability for CSPs with literals using the non-redundancy parameter NRD_n_(_R_), which roughly measures the largest instance in which every constraint is independently necessary. For the most general setting without literals, they obtained the corresponding characterization for Boolean relations and showed obstacles to extending their techniques to larger domains. Kol, Paramonov, Saxena, and Yu (ITCS 2023) similarly characterized the streaming complexity of Exact-CSP(_R_) for Boolean CSPs with literals in terms of the degree deg(_R_) of the relation when written as a polynomial, while without literals, the corresponding result was known only for Max-Cut. For all three of the objectives we study, we give tight characterizations for unweighted CSP instances over arbitrary finite domains. The streaming algorithms we provide are deterministic, while the corresponding bounds are tight up to polylogarithmic factors, even against randomized algorithms. The central idea in all three results is a reduction of _R_ to its core, a canonical subrelation of _R_ which admits gadgets that allow for the hard-pinning (or fixing) of variables. ∗Supported in part by NSF awards CCF-2211972 and DMS-2503280 and Venkatesan Guruswami’s Simons Investigator award. †Supported in part by a Jane Street Graduate Research Fellowship, Simons Investigator awards to Madhu Sudan and Salil Vadhan, and AFOSR award FA9550-25-1-0112. ‡Supported in part by NSERC Discovery grant RGPIN-2026-04689 and ECR supplement DGECR-2026-00421.

## 1 Introduction

Constraint satisfaction problems (CSPs) are one of the basic objects in theoretical computer science. Fix a finite domain _D_, an arity _k_, and a relation \(R\subseteq D^k\). An _R_-constraint applies _R_ to an ordered _k_-tuple of variables, with repetitions allowed, and an _R_-instance is a collection of such constraints. The basic satisfiability problem asks whether there is an assignment that satisfies every constraint. By varying the relation _R_, CSPs can capture a huge variety of natural problems, from bipartiteness, to 3-SAT, to graph coloring, and to systems of linear equations.

More recently, a line of work has emerged which studies the complexity of solving such CSPs in the _streaming model_. In this setting, each of the _m_ constraints is revealed one at a time. The goal, as before, is to decide satisfiability or a related objective for the resulting instance using _as little space_ as possible. We assume throughout that the stream length is polynomially bounded in _n_. Naturally, storing every constraint explicitly as it arrives allows one to store the entire CSP instance, meaning there is a trivial upper bound of _O(n<sup>k</sup>_log_n_) bits of space for any such task.

The streaming study of CSP optimization was initiated by Kapralov, Khanna, and Sudan [KKS15], who proved strong lower bounds for approximating Max-Cut. Kapralov and Krachun [KK19] subsequently proved that there is no non-trivial approximation for Max-Cut in sublinear-space in the streaming model. Guruswami, Velingker, and Velusamy [GVV17] and Chou, Golovnev, and Velusamy [CGV20] studied Boolean Max-CSPs of arity two, while Chou, Golovnev, Sudan, and Velusamy [CGSV24] extended this line of work to arbitrary finite Max-CSPs.

Very recently, this line of work has led to substantially broader characterizations of the streaming approximability of Max-CSPs. A sequence of works developed increasingly strong sublinear-space algorithms and lower bounds for Max-DiCut and Max-Cut [SSSV25; FMW25; Vel25; ABFS26], while Singer, Tulsiani, and Velusamy [STV25] and Fei, Minzer, and Wang [FMW26a] uncovered a close connection between streaming approximability and the standard BasicLP relaxation for CSPs. Subsequent works essentially completed this picture in the one-pass setting, giving sublinear-space algorithms up to the approximation threshold predicted by BasicLP and linear-space lower bounds beyond it [ABF26; STV26; FMW26b]. Thus, the streaming approximability of Max-CSPs is now understood to a remarkable extent, in sharp contrast to the objectives that we study in this work.

Kol, Paramonov, Saxena, and Yu [KPSY23] studied exact optimization for Boolean CSPs with literals. Their formulation asks, for a given threshold _v_, whether some assignment satisfies at least _v_ constraints, which is equivalent to computing the maximum number of satisfied constraints exactly. They showed that if the indicator of the predicate has polynomial degree _d_, then the streaming space complexity is \(\widetilde{\Theta}(n^d)\). Other work has focused on satisfiability. Vu [Vu24] proved an \(\Omega(n^k)\) lower bound for _k_-SAT, while Chou, Golovnev, Sudan, and Velusamy [CGSV24] proved an \(\Omega(n)\) lower bound for arbitrary CSPs.

The streaming complexity of satisfiability was characterized more recently by Sharma and Velusamy [SV26a], who showed that for a relation _R_, its space complexity is characterized, up to a logarithmic factor, by the non-redundancy of _R_. Non-redundancy in turn is a fundamental parameter in the study of CSPs, known to govern the query complexity of learning CSPs [BCK20; Car22], the kernelizability of CSPs [JP19; CJP20; LW20], and approximate sparsification of CSPs [KK15; FK17; BŽ20; KPS24; KPS25; BG25]. Given this rapidly-growing list of connections, there has been a recent surge of interest in obtaining sharp asymptotic estimates for the non-redundancy of many CSP predicates [BCK20; CJP20; LW20; Car22; KPS25; BG25; BGJ<sup>+</sup>25; LGE26; BGP26a; SV26b; BGJ<sup>+</sup>26], often combining ideas from logic, algebra, and extremal combinatorics. Recent work has obtained further bounds and structural results for non-redundancy and sparsification [BGP26b; BGP26c; BGP26d].

These characterizations rely crucially on the use of literals. In the general-domain literal model,<tbc>

the domain is Z_<sub>q</sub>_ and each occurrence of a variable may be replaced by \(x+\lambda\) for an arbitrary shift \(\lambda\in\mathbb{Z}_q\). Over the Boolean domain, these are precisely the two literals _x_ and \(\neg x\)<sup>1</sup>. Literals are more than a notational convenience in these arguments. Indeed, negations or additive shifts allow for much more powerful gadgets which lead to simpler lower bound proofs. Sharma and Velusamy \[SV26a\] showed that this is a fundamental obstruction in applying their techniques to general finite-domain CSPs. Over domains larger than two, the raw non-redundancy of _R_ need not predict the streaming complexity of CSP satisfiability.

The difficulty lies specifically in proving lower bounds. The known upper bounds continue to apply, since ordinary CSP instances are special cases of instances in the literal model. In the lower bound reductions however, literals were critical in gadget constructions that fixed the values of certain variables. Our starting question is therefore the following.

_Can we derive tight characterizations of the streaming complexity of_ CSPs?

As our primary contribution, we give an affirmative answer to the above question, in part making use of a crucial object called the _core_ of the CSP relation _R_, denoted by core(_R_), which intuitively removes domain values that can be collapsed without changing any of these objectives. In the context of CSPs, the notion of a core originated in the 1970s in the context of designing optimal queries to a database \[CM77; KV08\] but the concept was also independently developed in the graph theory literature (see \[HN92; HN08\]). Perhaps the most notable use of CSP cores is their key role in the proof of the CSP dichotomy theorem \[FV98; BKW17; Bul17; Zhu20\]. Despite these many connections, our work appears to be the first to utilize the concept of a CSP core in the context of streaming.

Beyond simply studying SAT(_R_), which asks whether all constraints can be satisfied, we also study Min-CSP(_R_), which approximately minimizes the number of unsatisfied constraints, and Exact-CSP(_R_), which computes the maximum number of satisfied constraints exactly. Thus, Exact-CSP(_R_) is the exact-value version of Max-CSP(_R_), and we use the latter terminology primarily for the approximation literature. As a byproduct of our study, we show that (a) non-redundancy is even more entrenched as a crucial parameter which governs the streaming complexity of CSP problems and (b) the core is a fundamental object which allows for the extension of lower bound techniques to general finite-domain CSPs.

## 1.1 Our Results

We study the one-pass streaming complexity of solving three different CSP objectives defined by a fixed finite relation _R_, namely SAT(_R_), Min-CSP(_R_), and Exact-CSP(_R_). The main parameter that governs the space complexity in our results is non-redundancy. Informally, an instance is non-redundant if every constraint is non-redundant, i.e., removing it would strictly grow the set of satisfying assignments of the instance. This is equivalent to having a witness assignment for each constraint that violates it but satisfies the rest of the constraints. We write NRD_<sub>n</sub>(R_) for the largest number of constraints in such an instance on _n_ variables. Our first theorem takes advantage of both NRD and core(_R_) and characterizes the randomized one-pass streaming complexity of SAT(_R_) up to a log factor.

**Theorem 1.1** (Informal Theorem 5.1 satisfiability characterization)**.** _For every fixed non-trivial relation R, there is a deterministic one-pass algorithm that solves_ SAT(_R_) _using O<sub>R</sub>_(NRD_<sub>n</sub>_(core(_R_))log_n_) _space, and any one-pass algorithm (even randomized) requires at least_ \(\Omega_R(\mathsf{NRD}_n(\mathsf{core}(R)))\) _space._

<sup>1</sup>By the general finite-domain setting, we mean that the relation and its finite domain are arbitrary, and constraints apply the relation directly to variables, without literals or shifts.

Our minimization result comes from a stronger sparsification theorem, resembling those of \[KPS24; KPS25; BG25\]. The goal here is, given a CSP instance _C_, to build a small, re-weighted sub- instance (denoted \(\hat{C}\)) such that on _every assignment_ \((x_1,\dots,x_n)\in D^n\), the number of unsatisfied constraints in \(\hat{C}\) is essentially the same as the number of unsatisfied constraints in _C_. Clearly, once such a sparsifier is constructed, one can (approximately) solve Min-CSP(_R_). Importantly, we show that building and maintaining such sparsifiers can still be done in space roughly equal to the non-redundancy:

**Theorem 1.2** (Informal Theorem 6.1 and Corollary 6.2 sparsification and minimization characterization)**.** _For every fixed non-trivial relation R and every_ \(\varepsilon>0\)_, there is a deterministic one-pass algorithm that can store a_ \((1\pm\varepsilon)\) _sparsifier using_ \(O_{R,\varepsilon}(\mathsf{NRD}_n(R)\mathrm{poly}(\mathrm{log}n))\) _space. Consequently, there is a deterministic one-pass_ \((1+\varepsilon)\)_-approximation algorithm for_ Min-CSP(_R_) _using_ \(O_{R,\varepsilon}(\mathsf{NRD}_n(\mathrm{core}(R))\mathrm{poly}(\mathrm{log}n))\) _space, and every finite-factor randomized approximation requires_ \(\Omega_R(\mathsf{NRD}_n(\mathrm{core}(R)))\) _space._

Finally, for Exact-CSP, the space complexity is determined by the polynomial degree of the core<sup>2</sup>.

**Theorem 1.3** (Informal Theorem 7.1 Exact-CSP characterization)**.** _Let d be the degree of the indicator function of_ core(_R). Solving_ Exact-CSP(_R_) _in one pass on simple instances requires_ \(\Omega_R(n^d)\) _randomized space and has a deterministic O<sub>R</sub>(n<sup>d</sup>_log_n)-space algorithm._

Thus all three problems first reduce to the core. After that reduction, non-redundancy characterizes satisfiability and minimization up to polylogarithmic factors, while degree characterizes Exact-CSP up to a logarithmic factor.

## The Core

The reason that core(_R_) is central to each of these results is due to the core being the _canonical fixed-point_ of _R_ under homomorphisms. More precisely, given a finite domain _D_ and a relation \(R\subseteq D^k\), a homomorphism of _R_ to itself is a map \(h:D\rightarrow D\) such that for every tuple \((t_1,\dots,t_k)\in R\), we have that \((h(t_1),\dots,h(t_k))\in R\). Given an _R_-instance of a CSP, a homomorphism _h_ always maps a satisfying assignment to a satisfying assignment. Furthermore, in the optimization setting, applying a homomorphism to an arbitrary assignment cannot decrease the number of satisfied constraints. Therefore, in any of our streaming problems, we may apply any homomorphism we desire at no cost.

If the map _h_ is not a bijection, then _h_ maps _R_ to a smaller-domain relation _h(R_). Since the domain _D_ is finite, such a shrinking can only be done a finite number of times until a fixed point is reached-this is precisely the core of the relation. As such, for any of our streaming problems, an algorithm for core(_R_) is a natural upper bound on the problem. A corresponding lower bound follows from the fact that CSP cores have canonical gadgets that can be used to fix variables. Further<tbc>

<sup>2</sup>More formally, if _C_ is the domain of the core, we write our predicate core(_R_) as a real-valued indicator function \(f:C^k\rightarrow\mathbb{R}\), compute its Fourier decomposition, and let _d_ be degree of the highest-degree monomial with a non-zero coefficient.
