## 2 Technical overview

In this section, we explain the main structural ideas behind our results. Our central idea is to replace every relation by a reduced form called its _core_, which we define formally in Section 3.4. We first use a relation of Sharma and Velusamy \[SV26a\] to explain why we must reduce to the core. We then explain the satisfiability lower bound using CUT={(0,1),(1,0)} and return to CUT to explain the exact optimization lower bound. As we will show, the satisfiability and exact-optimization lower bounds crucially rely on whether we can _hard-pin_ variables, meaning fix them to chosen values in the domain. _R_-constraints usually cannot do this directly, so we instead build gadgets that simulate such pinnings up to unavoidable symmetries of the relation. The main fact that makes these gadgets possible is that the relation is a core. For satisfiability, we need a gadget whose satisfying assignments give the variables the desired values. For exact optimization, an optimal assignment may violate some gadget constraints, so we need a stronger construction that makes every deviation from the desired values unprofitable.

### 2.1 Reduction to the core

Sharma and Velusamy \[SV26a\] proved that the one-pass space needed to decide satisfiability for CSPs with literals is characterized, up to a logarithmic factor, by the _non-redundancy_ parameter NRD_<sub>n</sub>(R_). This parameter is the maximum number of constraints in an _R_-instance in which every constraint is independently necessary. Equivalently, every constraint has a _witness assignment_ that violates it and satisfies all the other constraints. We give the formal definition in Section 3.3.

They also showed that without literals, NRD_<sub>n</sub>(R_) need not be the right parameter, using the following counterexample<tbc>

\(T=\{(0,1),(1,0),(0,3),(3,0),(1,2),(2,1)\}\subseteq\{0,1,2,3\}^2.\)

<tbc>Using known characterizations of non-redundancy, one can prove that \(\mathsf{NRD}_n(T)=\Theta(n^2)\) \[BŽ20; BCK20; KPS25; SV26a\]. However, satisfiability for _T_ can be checked in _O(n_log_n_) space. To see this, notice that _T(a,b_) holds when _a_ and _b_ have opposite parity and at least one of them belongs to {0,1}. Given a _T_-instance, form its underlying graph whose vertices are the variables and whose edges are the pairs {_x,y_} on which a constraint _T(x,y_) appears. The _T_-instance is satisfiable exactly when this graph is bipartite. Indeed, every satisfying assignment gives a bipartition according to the parity of the assigned values. Conversely, any bipartition can be made satisfying by assigning 0 to one side and 1 to the other. Bipartiteness can be decided in one pass using _O(n_log_n_) bits \[SV26a\].

This suggests that the values 2 and 3 are unnecessary for solving the instance. So, let’s consider the map<tbc>

\(\sigma(0)=\sigma(2)=0\text{and}\sigma(1)=\sigma(3)=1.\)

If \((a,b)\in T\), then _a_ and _b_ have opposite parity. Therefore \((\sigma(a),\sigma(b))\) is either (0,1) or (1,0) and still belongs to _T_. Applying \(\sigma\) to an assignment therefore preserves every constraint that was already satisfied. Thus every assignment can be replaced by a Boolean assignment satisfying at least the same constraints.

The restriction of _T_ to {0,1} is precisely CUT={(0,1),(1,0)}. In this sense, _T_ is essentially the same relation as CUT. Every assignment over the original domain can be mapped to a Boolean assignment without losing a satisfied constraint, while every Boolean assignment is already available over the original domain. It follows that restricting the domain to {0,1} preserves satisfiability, the minimum number of unsatisfied constraints, and the maximum number of satisfied constraints. This is also the reason the bipartiteness argument above works, but the map \(\sigma\) states it in a form that extends to every relation.

Formally, a map that preserves a relation in this way is called an _endomorphism_, defined formally in Section 3.4. The _core_ of a relation is obtained by choosing an endomorphism with the smallest possible image and restricting the relation to that image. In this example, \(\sigma\) has image {0,1}, and no endomorphism can have a one-element image because _T_ contains no pair (_a,a_). We therefore have core(_T_)=CUT.

Notice that \(\mathsf{NRD}_n(\mathsf{CUT})=\Theta(n)\). If a CUT-instance is satisfiable and nonredundant, its graph must be a forest because every edge on a cycle is implied by the remaining edges. If it is unsatisfiable and nonredundant, removing any edge must make it bipartite, so its nonisolated part is an odd cycle. In either case it has _O(n_) edges, while a forest gives the matching lower bound. Reducing to the core therefore replaces the incorrect quadratic parameter NRD_<sub>n</sub>(T_) by the correct linear parameter NRD_<sub>n</sub>_(CUT).

The examples above suggest the following general statement, which we prove formally in Section 4.

**Theorem 2.1** (Informal Lemmas 4.2 and 4.3)**.** _For every relation R, replacing each R-constraint by the_ core(_R)-constraint on the same scope preserves satisfiability, the minimum number of unsatisfied constraints, and the maximum number of satisfied constraints. Consequently, this replacement preserves the one-pass streaming space of all three problems we consider._

Moreover, this reduction can be performed as the stream arrives. Whenever an _R_-constraint appears, we replace it by the core(_R_)-constraint on the same scope and give it to the algorithm for the core relation.

Now, the remaining task is to prove tight space bounds for the core relation. The satisfiability upper bound now follows immediately. We reduce the stream to the core and apply the algorithm of Sharma and Velusamy [SV26a], which uses _O<sub>R</sub>_(NRD_<sub>n</sub>_(core(_R_))log_n_) space. As we will see later in Section 2.3, the upper bound for exact-optimization follows as well using a simple argument. It remains to prove the lower bound matching this up to the logarithmic factor.

For both the lower bounds, we use the standard connection between streaming algorithms and one-way communication together with the hard problem INDEX, where Alice receives a string \(b\in\{0,1\}^m\) and Bob receives an index _j_ and must recover _b<sub>j</sub>_. At a high level, we reduce this communication problem to a streaming problem as follows. Alice runs the streaming algorithm on constraints determined by her input and sends its memory state to Bob. Bob then appends constraints determined by his query and uses the output to recover the answer. The difficulty is that every constraint Bob appends must be a constraint of the core relation. He cannot directly fix variables to the values determined by his query. The next subsection explains how the core property lets him simulate this operation for satisfiability. The corresponding construction for exact optimization will require a stronger version of the same idea.

## 2.2 Satisfiability and hard pinning

We now explain why every one-pass algorithm for satisfiability over a core relation _R_ requires \(\Omega_R(\mathsf{NRD}_n(R))\) space, as stated formally in Theorem 5.3. The proof first gives an ideal reduction in which Bob can fix variables to chosen values. We then use CUT to see why unique fixing is sometimes impossible and what weaker property is enough. Finally, we state the general hard-pinning lemma for core relations.

Let _I_={_C_<sub>1</sub>_,...,C<sub>m</sub>_} be a maximum _nonredundant instance_ over a core relation _R_, where _m_=NRD_<sub>n</sub>(R_). Recall from Section 3.3 that every constraint _C<sub>j</sub>_ has a _witness assignment_ \(\alpha_j\) that violates _C<sub>j</sub>_ and satisfies every other constraint in _I_.

In INDEX, Alice receives a string \(b\in\{0,1\}^m\) and inserts _C<sub>i</sub>_ whenever _b<sub>i</sub>_=1. Bob receives an index _j_ and must recover _b<sub>j</sub>_. If Bob could append constraints that _hard-pin_ every variable to the value given by \(\alpha_j\), meaning that the appended constraints force this assignment, then the reduction would be immediate. If _b<sub>j</sub>_=0, the witness \(\alpha_j\) satisfies Alice’s entire instance. If _b<sub>j</sub>_=1, Alice also inserted _C<sub>j</sub>_, which \(\alpha_j\) violates. Thus the final instance would be satisfiable exactly when _b<sub>j</sub>_=0.

The obstacle is that _R_-constraints may not be able to force a unique assignment. The following example shows both the obstacle and the weaker form of pinning that we need.

**Example 2.2** (Hard pinning for CUT)**.** Consider _R_=CUT. Complementing every value preserves every constraint, so any instance satisfied by \(\alpha_j\) is also satisfied by its complement. Bob does not need uniqueness, however. It is enough to append an instance whose satisfying assignments on the original variables are \(\alpha_j\) and its complement.

Bob introduces two dummy variables _z_<sub>0</sub>_,z_<sub>1</sub> and adds the constraint CUT(_z_<sub>0</sub>_,z_<sub>1</sub>). For every original variable _x_, he adds CUT(_x,z_<sub>1</sub>) if \(\alpha_j(x)=0\) and CUT(_x,z_<sub>0</sub>) if \(\alpha_j(x)=1\). Any assignment satisfying these constraints must give _z_<sub>0</sub> and _z_<sub>1</sub> different values. Once those two values are chosen, every original variable is forced. The assignment on the original variables is therefore either \(\alpha_j\) or its complement.

This completes the reduction for CUT. If _b<sub>j</sub>_=0, the assignment \(\alpha_j\) satisfies Alice’s constraints and Bob’s constraints. If _b<sub>j</sub>_=1, Alice inserted _C<sub>j</sub>_, which is violated by \(\alpha_j\). Its complement also violates _C<sub>j</sub>_ because complementing every value preserves whether a CUT-constraint is satisfied. Hence the final instance is satisfiable exactly when _b<sub>j</sub>_=0.

The map that swaps 0 and 1 is an endomorphism of CUT that only permutes its values. Such a bijective endomorphism is called an _automorphism_. Applying an automorphism to every value preserves every constraint, which explains why the unavoidable ambiguity between \(\alpha_j\) and its complement is harmless.

The CUT example shows that Bob does not need to force one assignment uniquely. It is enough to force all original variables according to the same symmetry of the relation. For a core relation, every endomorphism is an automorphism, and this is precisely the property that makes the general construction work.

**Lemma 2.3** (Informal Lemma 4.4)**.** _Let R be a core relation and let_ \(\alpha\) _be an assignment to a set of variables. There is an R-instance whose satisfying assignments on these variables are exactly the assignments_ \(\pi\circ\alpha\)_, where the same automorphism_ \(\pi\) _of R is applied to every variable._

Here is the idea behind the lemma. Introduce one dummy variable _y<sub>a</sub>_ for every value _a_ in the domain. Add constraints among these variables so that, under any satisfying assignment, the map sending _a_ to the value of _y<sub>a</sub>_ preserves _R_ and is therefore an endomorphism. Since _R_ is a core relation, this map must be an automorphism. We then attach every original variable _x_ to these<tbc>

dummy variables so that _x_ must receive the image of \(\alpha(x)\) under the same automorphism. Thus all original variables follow one common symmetry of _R_.

Every assignment \(\pi\circ\alpha_j\) satisfies and violates exactly the same _R_-constraints as \(\alpha_j\). Bob can therefore append the instance from the informal lemma in the ideal reduction above. If _b<sub>j</sub>_=0, an automorphic image of \(\alpha_j\) satisfies the final instance. If _b<sub>j</sub>_=1, every assignment satisfying Bob’s constraints violates _C<sub>j</sub>_. A streaming algorithm for satisfiability would therefore give a one-way protocol for INDEX_<sub>m</sub>_, proving the \(\Omega_R(\text{NRD}_n(R))\) lower bound for core relations. Reducing an arbitrary relation to its core gives the characterization in Section 5.

For the sake of brevity, we next discuss the techniques that underlie the Exact-CSP results. For a discussion of the sparsification and minimization results, we encourage the reader to look at Section 6.

## 2.3 Exact-CSP

We now explain why exact optimization requires a stronger pinning construction than satisfiability. Let _d_ be the _degree_ of the indicator function of the core relation. Informally, this is the largest number of coordinates that occur together in a monomial of its polynomial representation. Our result gives an _O<sub>R</sub>(n<sup>d</sup>_log_n_) upper bound and a matching \(\Omega_R(n^d)\) lower bound up to the logarithmic factor. The formal statement is Theorem 7.1, and the formal definition of degree is in Section 3.5.

As before, we first reduce the relation to its core. The upper bound stores the coefficients of the low-degree polynomial representing the value of the instance. For the lower bound, the ideal reduction again asks Bob to hard-pin complete assignments. It is tempting to use Lemma 4.4 for this purpose. But that lemma is not strong enough here. It describes assignments that satisfy every pinning constraint, whereas an optimal assignment may violate some pinning constraints in order to satisfy more of Alice’s constraints. We therefore first describe the ideal reduction and then explain how a stronger pinning construction ensures that such a violation cannot improve the objective.

**Example 2.4** (Degree of CUT)**.** For CUT on the domain {0,1}, the indicator is **1**<sub>CUT</sub>(_x,y_)=_x+y_-2_xy_. Its degree is therefore 2.

**Example 2.5** (Degree of NAE)**.** Let \(R_\text{NAE}\subseteq\{0,1\}^3\) contain the tuples whose three entries are not all equal. Its indicator is **1**<sub>_R_NAE</sub>(_x,y,z_)=_x+y+z-xy-xz-yz_. Thus _R_NAE has degree 2 even though its arity is 3.

### Upper bound.

The upper bound follows directly from the polynomial representation. Kol, Paramonov, Saxena, and Yu \[KPSY23\] give the Boolean version. They write the value of an instance as a polynomial in the variables and store its coefficients. Each arriving constraint adds one fixed low-degree polynomial to this coefficient table. We use the same idea over an arbitrary finite domain, using the value indicators from Section 3.5 in place of Boolean variables.

**Example 2.6** (The upper bound for CUT)**.** Consider a stream of edges defining a CUT-instance. By the expansion above, an arriving edge {_x<sub>u</sub>,x<sub>v</sub>_} contributes _x<sub>u</sub>+x<sub>v</sub>_-2_x<sub>u</sub>x<sub>v</sub>_ to the value of every assignment. The algorithm adds these three coefficients to its table. After the stream, the sum of the stored terms is exactly the number of edges cut by every assignment. There are only _O(n_<sup>2</sup>) possible terms, and their coefficients use _O_(log_n_) bits on a simple instance. The algorithm may then try every assignment, evaluate the stored polynomial, and return its maximum. Thus Exact-CSP(CUT) uses _O(n_<sup>2</sup>log_n_) space.

The same argument works over every finite domain. If the indicator of the core relation has degree _d_, each arriving constraint contributes a fixed polynomial whose terms involve at most _d_ variables. Across all scopes, there are only _O<sub>R</sub>(n<sup>d</sup>_) possible terms. The algorithm stores the coefficient of each term, and after the stream it tries all assignments and returns the largest value. This gives the _O<sub>R</sub>(n<sup>d</sup>_log_n_) upper bound and extends the Boolean argument of Kol, Paramonov, Saxena, and Yu to arbitrary finite domains.

## The lower bound.

We again reduce from one-way INDEX. We call the values of Alice’s instance at assignments chosen by Bob _point evaluations_. The following CUT example shows how degree lets Bob combine these point evaluations to recover his bit.

**Example 2.7** (Four point evaluations for CUT)**.** Alice receives bits _b<sub>ij</sub>_ indexed by \((i,j)\in[N]^2\). She creates vertices _x_<sub>1</sub>_,...,x<sub>N</sub>_ and _y_<sub>1</sub>_,...,y<sub>N</sub>_, and inserts the edge {_x<sub>i</sub>,y<sub>j</sub>_} whenever _b<sub>ij</sub>_=1. Let _P_ denote the resulting graph.

Bob receives a pair (_p,q_). He uses four assignments. The assignment _s_<sub>00</sub> sets every variable to 0. The assignment _s_<sub>10</sub> sets only _x<sub>p</sub>_ to 1, the assignment _s_<sub>01</sub> sets only _y<sub>q</sub>_ to 1, and the assignment _s_<sub>11</sub> sets only _x<sub>p</sub>_ and _y<sub>q</sub>_ to 1. In the ideal reduction, Bob makes four copies of Alice’s streaming state and appends a different input to each copy, one for each of these assignments. The four point evaluations satisfy

\(\text{val}_P(s_{11})-\text{val}_P(s_{10})-\text{val}_P(s_{01})+\text{val}_P(s_{00})=-2b_{pq}.\)

To see the cancellation, consider one edge of _P_. An edge not incident to _x<sub>p</sub>_ or _y<sub>q</sub>_ contributes zero to the signed sum. An edge incident to exactly one of them contributes equally to two terms with opposite signs. The only edge that can remain is {_x<sub>p</sub>,y<sub>q</sub>_}. If it is present, it is cut under _s_<sub>10</sub> and _s_<sub>01</sub> but not under _s_<sub>00</sub> or _s_<sub>11</sub>, giving a total contribution of -2.

Thus Bob can recover _b<sub>pq</sub>_ if the run from each copy reveals the value of _P_ at its chosen assignment. If Bob could directly hard-pin the chosen assignment, he could append the required constraints in each run. For CUT, it is enough to force either that assignment or its complement, since complementation preserves the value of every CUT-instance. The optimum of the resulting instance, after subtracting the known number of pinning constraints, would reveal the required point evaluation.

Roughly, the same ideal reduction extends to every core relation of degree _d_. Alice’s bits are indexed by [_N]<sup>d</sup>_, and Bob considers 2_<sup>d</sup>_ assignments obtained by changing the selected variable in each of _d_ groups. A signed sum of their values cancels every constraint except the one indexed by Bob’s query. If Bob could hard-pin each assignment in one run of the streaming algorithm, these 2_<sup>d</sup>_ optimum values would reveal his bit.

It would be tempting to use the same satisfiability hard-pinning lemma, Lemma 4.4. However, it only controls assignments that satisfy the whole pinning instance. An optimum for the exact- optimization problem might instead violate one pinning constraint and gain many constraints from Alice’s instance. We therefore replace the constant-size pinning gadget by large blocks whose constraints outweigh every possible gain from _P_.

**Example 2.8** (Strong pinning for CUT)**.** The graph _P_ has 2_N_ vertices, at most _N_<sup>2</sup> edges, and maximum degree at most _N_. Fix an assignment _s_ to its vertices. We want to add a gadget that forces every optimum to agree with _s_ on the original vertices, up to complementing every value. To do this, we introduce extra vertices. Let _L_=1000_N_, and create two blocks _Z_<sub>0</sub>_,Z_<sub>1</sub>, each containing<tbc>

<tbc>_L_ vertices. Add every edge between the two blocks. For every original vertex _x_, add 10_N_ edges from _x_ to distinct vertices in _Z_<sub>1</sub> when _s(x_)=0, and to distinct vertices in _Z_<sub>0</sub> when _s(x_)=1.

We first show that every optimum makes the two blocks monochromatic, meaning that all vertices in each block receive the same value, and gives the blocks opposite values. Choose a most frequent value in each block. If these two values are the same, at least _L_<sup>2</sup>/4 edges between the blocks are uncut. Making the blocks monochromatic with opposite values cuts all block edges and loses at most the 20_N_<sup>2</sup> edges attached to the original vertices. Since _L_<sup>2</sup>/4_\>_20_N_<sup>2</sup>, an optimum must have opposite majority values. Up to complementing the entire cut, assume that the majority value of _Z_<sub>0</sub> is 0 and that of _Z_<sub>1</sub> is 1.

Let _a_ be the number of vertices assigned 1 in _Z_<sub>0</sub>, and let _c_ be the number assigned 0 in _Z_<sub>1</sub>. The number of uncut edges between the blocks is \(a(L-c)+(L-a)c=L(a+c)-2ac\ge L(a+c)/2\). Making both blocks monochromatic according to their majority values gains these edges and loses at most 2_N(a+c_) attached edges. Since _L/_2_\>_2_N_, an optimum must have _a=c_=0. Thus _Z_<sub>0</sub> is entirely 0 and _Z_<sub>1</sub> is entirely 1, up to complementing all values.

Once the blocks are fixed, every original vertex _x_ receives all its 10_N_ attached edges exactly when _x=s(x_). Giving _x_ the other value loses 10_N_ attached edges and can gain at most its _N_ incident edges in _P_. Hence every optimum agrees with _s_ on all original vertices, up to complementing the whole assignment.

Let _H<sub>s</sub>_ denote the block and attached edges. The intended assignment cuts every edge of _H<sub>s</sub>_, and complementation preserves the value of every CUT-instance. Therefore

\(\mathrm{OPT}_\mathrm{max}(P\cup H_s)=|H_s|+\mathrm{val}_P(s).\)

The construction depends only on the public value _N_ and on _s_, so Bob can build it without knowing which edges Alice inserted.

Bob now makes four copies of Alice’s streaming state and appends _H_<sub>_s_<sub>00</sub></sub>, _H_<sub>_s_<sub>10</sub></sub>, _H_<sub>_s_<sub>01</sub></sub>, and _H_<sub>_s_<sub>11</sub></sub> to the respective copies. From each optimum, he subtracts the known size of the appended gadget and obtains one point evaluation of _P_. Their alternating sum reveals _b<sub>pq</sub>_, giving an \(\Omega(N^2)\) lower bound for Exact-CSP(CUT).<sup>3</sup>

For a general core relation of degree _d_, the construction in Lemma 4.6 plays the same role. It replaces the two CUT blocks by one block for every value in the core domain. The constraints among the blocks force their most frequent values to define one common endomorphism, which must be an automorphism because the relation is a core. The attached constraints then force the original variables to follow the desired assignment under this automorphism. As in the CUT example, the blocks are large enough that every deviation loses more attached constraints than it can gain in Alice’s instance.

The formal construction gives exactly the property needed in the communication reduction.

**Lemma 2.9** (Informal Lemma 4.6)**.** _Let R be a core relation, and let P be a simple R-instance on O<sub>R</sub>(N_) _variables with at most N<sup>d</sup> constraints and maximum variable degree at most N_<sup>_d_-1</sup>_. For every assignment s to the variables of P, there is an R-instance H<sub>s</sub>, using O<sub>R</sub>(N_) _additional variables and constructible without knowing the constraints of P, such that_ \(\mathrm{OPT}_\mathrm{max}(P\cup H_s)=|H_s|+\mathrm{val}_P(s)\).

Alice’s instance and each pinning gadget use only _O<sub>R</sub>(N_) variables. Bob can therefore recover the 2_<sup>d</sup>_ point evaluations needed by the signed sum, and the lower bound for INDEX<sub>_N<sup>d</sup>_</sub> gives the \(\Omega_R(n^d)\) space lower bound.

<sup>3</sup>Kol, Paramonov, Saxena, and Yu \[KPSY23\] also prove an ad hoc \(\Omega(n^2)\) lower bound for Max-Cut via a different reduction.

The two lower bounds therefore use the same structural principle. We first reduce exactly to the core and then recover the variable pinnings. For satisfiability, it is enough to restrict the satisfying assignments up to one common automorphism. For exact optimization, the restriction must additionally be strong enough that violating it is never profitable. The sparsification result uses the same core reduction to obtain the minimization characterization.

### 2.4 Relation to prior work

We first explain how our results extend the earlier work of Sharma and Velusamy [SV26a]. Here, a constraint language is a fixed finite set of relations over the same domain. They proved the satisfiability characterization in two settings. First, they considered every finite domain but allowed literals: when the domain is Z_<sub>q</sub>_, each occurrence of a variable _x_ in a constraint may be replaced by \(x+\lambda\) modulo _q_, for an arbitrary \(\lambda\in\mathbb{Z}_q\). In the Boolean setting, this is exactly the choice between _x_ and \(\neg x\). These shifts give the lower bound construction more freedom. For a fixed relation, a lower bound that uses nonzero shifts need not apply when all shifts are zero.

Their second result concerns positive Boolean CSPs, meaning Boolean CSPs without literals. They assume that the constraint language is not "constant-satisfiable". This means that there is no value \(c\in\{0,1\}\) for which assigning every variable the value _c_ satisfies every relation in the language. This is the general interesting case for positive Boolean CSPs, since otherwise every instance has the same constant satisfying assignment.

**Lemma 2.10** (Informal Lemmas A.2 and A.7)**.** _Reducing a language with literals to its core does not change its non-redundancy. Moreover, a Boolean constraint language is a core if and only if it is not constant-satisfiable._

Our core viewpoint uses these two facts to explain both earlier results. For the literal model, treat every shifted use of a relation as a separate relation. The resulting language is shift-closed, so the first part of the lemma shows that passing to its core does not change its non-redundancy. Our general core characterization therefore gives the earlier characterization for CSPs with literals. For the positive Boolean result, the only non-bijective maps on the Boolean domain are the two constant maps, which send both domain values to 0 or both to 1. The second part of the lemma therefore shows that the assumption of not being constant-satisfiable is exactly the assumption that the language is a core.

Our work then goes beyond both results by giving a characterization in the most general finite-domain setting. The precise statements and their proofs are given in Section A.

We also compare our exact-optimization result with the work of Kol, Paramonov, Saxena, and Yu [KPSY23]. Their general characterization is restricted to Boolean CSPs with literals and constants. Our result applies to arbitrary relations, requiring neither literals nor constants, giving a characterization in the more general CSP setting. However, their lower bound does extend to a constant number of passes. We view an extension of our result to the multi-pass setting as an exciting future direction.

## 3 Preliminaries

In this section, we state the definitions used in the rest of the paper.

## 3.1 CSPs

Throughout the paper, _D_ is a fixed finite nonempty domain and \(R\subseteq D^k\) is a fixed relation of arity \(k\ge 1\). We work with ordinary _R_-constraints, without literals or shifts. We refer to this as the general finite-domain setting, since the finite domain and relation are arbitrary. We call _R non-trivial_ if \(\varnothing\unknown R\unknown D^k\). The asymptotic symbols _O<sub>R</sub>_, \(\Omega_R\), and \(\Theta_R\) hide constants that may depend on _R_.

Let _V_={_x_<sub>1</sub>_,...,x<sub>n</sub>_} be a set of variables. An _R-constraint_ is an expression _R(x_<sub>_i_<sub>1</sub></sub>_,...,x<sub>i<sub>k</sub></sub>_), and its _scope_ is the ordered variable tuple (_x_<sub>_i_<sub>1</sub></sub>_,...,x<sub>i<sub>k</sub></sub>_). The order matters unless _R_ is symmetric. Variables may repeat within a scope. An assignment \(\alpha:V\rightarrow D\) satisfies this constraint if \((\alpha(x_{i_1}),\dots,\alpha(x_{i_k}))\in R\).

An unweighted _R_-instance _I_ is a finite multiset of _R_-constraints. Thus the same constraint may occur more than once, and |_I_| counts constraints with multiplicity. A weighted instance gives every occurrence of a constraint _C_ a nonnegative rational weight _w(C_) represented in binary. Unweighted instances are the special case in which every weight is 1. The support of a weighted instance is the set of constraint occurrences with nonzero weight. A weighted subinstance \(H\subseteq I\) uses only occurrences from _I_, but it may give them new nonnegative weights.

An instance is _simple_ if no ordered scope occurs more than once. The degree of a variable is the number of constraint occurrences whose scopes contain it. A constraint contributes once to this degree even if the variable appears more than once in its scope. The maximum variable degree is denoted by \(\Delta(I)\). A relation is _symmetric_ if membership in _R_ is unchanged by permuting the _k_ coordinates. For a symmetric relation, we also use the stronger notion of _unordered simplicity_. This means that no two scopes become the same multiset of variables after their coordinates are reordered.

**Example 3.1.** Let _D_={0,1} and CUT={(0,1),(1,0)}. A CUT-constraint CUT(_x,y_) requires _x_ and _y_ to receive different values. Thus a CUT-instance is a graph, with one variable at each vertex and one constraint at each edge.

## 3.2 Objectives and streaming space

We next define the three objectives studied in the paper. We state them for a weighted _R_-instance, which is the more general setting. The inputs to our three problems are unweighted unless we say otherwise. Let _I_ be a weighted _R_-instance and let \(\alpha\) be an assignment to its variables. We write<tbc>

\(\text{val}_I(\alpha)=\sum_{C\in I\alpha\text{satisfies}C}w(C)\text{and}\text{unsatval}_I(\alpha)=\sum_{C\in I\alpha\text{violates}C}w(C).\)

<tbc>Thus \(\text{val}_I(\alpha)\) is the weight of the satisfied constraints and \(\text{unsatval}_I(\alpha)\) is the weight of the violated constraints. We define

\(\text{OPT}_\text{max}(I)=max_\alpha\text{val}_I(\alpha)\text{and}\text{OPT}_\text{min}(I)=min_\alpha\text{unsatval}_I(\alpha).\)

The set of satisfying assignments is \(\text{Sat}(I)=\{\alpha:\text{unsatval}_I(\alpha)=0\}\).

The problem SAT(_R_) asks whether Sat(_I_) is nonempty. The problem Min-CSP(_R_) asks for OPT<sub>min</sub>(_I_), and a \(\gamma\)-approximation must return a number between OPT<sub>min</sub>(_I_) and \(\gamma\text{OPT}_\text{min}(I)\). We write \(\text{Min-CSP}_\gamma(R)\) for this approximation problem. Finally, Exact-CSP(_R_) asks for the exact value OPT<sub>max</sub>(_I_). Instances are unweighted unless we explicitly say otherwise.

We will also use a stronger guarantee than merely approximating OPT<sub>min</sub>(_I_). A weighted subinstance \(H\subseteq I\) is a \((1\pm\varepsilon)\) _sparsifier_ of _I_ if \((1-\varepsilon)\text{unsatval}_I(\alpha)\le\text{unsatval}_H(\alpha)\le(1+\)<tbc>

\(\varepsilon)\text{unsatval}_I(\alpha)\text{for every assignment}\alpha\text{. As we show in Corollary 6.2, running the sparsifier with a slightly smaller error and minimizing these inequalities gives a}(1+\varepsilon)\text{-approximation to OPT}_\mathrm{min}(I)\text{.}\)

In the streaming model, the constraints arrive one at a time in an arbitrary order, and the algorithm makes one pass over this insertion-only stream. The domain and relation are fixed and are not part of the stream. We use _n_ for the number of variables and _m_ for the stream length. There is no restriction on the update time or on the time used after the stream. We measure only the number of stored bits.

Unless stated otherwise, a randomized algorithm must be correct with probability at least 2/3 on every input. We write SPACE(\(\Pi\)) for the minimum worst-case space of such a one-pass algorithm for a problem \(\Pi\). Upper bounds described as deterministic use no randomness, while all lower bounds also apply to randomized bounded-error algorithms.

## 3.3 Non-redundancy

Non-redundancy measures how many constraints can be independently necessary for satisfiability. Let _I_ be an unweighted _R_-instance and let \(C\in I\). We call _C redundant in I_ if every assignment satisfying all constraints obtained by removing this occurrence of _C_ also satisfies _C_. Otherwise, there is an assignment that violates _C_ and satisfies every other constraint of _I_. We call such an assignment a _witness for C_. The instance _I_ is _nonredundant_ if every one of its constraints has a witness.

We define NRD_<sub>n</sub>(R_) to be the maximum number of constraints in a nonredundant _R_-instance on at most _n_ variables.

**Example 3.2.** For the relation CUT, every forest gives a nonredundant instance. Fix an edge and remove it. The two endpoints are now in different components. We can properly 2-color each component and choose the colors so that these endpoints receive the same value. This assignment violates the removed edge and satisfies every other edge, so it is a witness for that edge.

We will use the following elementary lower bound to account for the space needed to store an assignment.

**Observation 3.3.** _If_ \(R\unknown D^k\) _is nonempty, then_ \(\mathsf{NRD}_n(R)=\Omega_R(n)\).

_Proof._ Choose a tuple \(r\in R\) and a tuple \(u\in D^k\backslash R\). Partition \(k\lfloor n/k\rfloor\) variables into disjoint ordered scopes of size _k_, and put one _R_-constraint on each scope. To witness one chosen constraint, assign the tuple _u_ to its scope and the tuple _r_ to every other scope. The chosen constraint is violated and all other constraints are satisfied. The resulting instance is nonredundant and has \(\lfloor n/k\rfloor=\Omega_R(n)\) constraints.

By definition, a non-trivial relation is nonempty and is not equal to _D<sup>k</sup>_. Thus the observation shows that non-redundancy is at least linear for every non-trivial fixed relation, although it may be much larger. Our satisfiability and minimization results depend on its value for the core of _R_, which we define next.

## 3.4 Cores, automorphisms, and hard pinnings

We now define the core of a relation. A map \(\sigma:D\rightarrow D\) is an _endomorphism_ of _R_ if applying \(\sigma\) to every coordinate of a tuple in _R_ always gives another tuple in _R_. Equivalently, \(\sigma(R)\subseteq R\). An endomorphism is an _automorphism_ if it is a bijection. In this case \(\sigma(R)=R\). We write Aut(_R_) for the set of automorphisms of _R_.

An endomorphism \(\sigma\) is _idempotent_ if \(\sigma(\sigma(a))=\sigma(a)\) for every \(a\in D\). Choose an endomorphism with minimum image. Its restriction to its image is a permutation, since applying the map again cannot make the image smaller. A suitable power is therefore the identity on its image and is idempotent. We fix such an idempotent endomorphism \(\sigma\) and write \(C=\sigma(D)\). We define

\(\mathrm{core}(R)=\sigma(R)=R\cap C^k,\)

and call _C_ its _core domain_. We fix one such choice throughout the paper. The equality holds because an idempotent map fixes every value in its image. The relation core(_R_) is a core relation because every one of its endomorphisms is an automorphism. Indeed, a non-bijective endomorphism composed with \(\sigma\) would give an endomorphism of _R_ with image smaller than _C_. We call _R_ itself a _core relation_ when every endomorphism of _R_ is an automorphism.

**Example 3.4.** For CUT, every endomorphism must send 0 and 1 to different values. Hence its only endomorphisms are the identity and the map that swaps 0 and 1. Both are automorphisms, so CUT is a core relation.

For a relation that is not a core, let _D_={0,1,2} and let

\(R_\mathrm{star}=\{(0,1),(1,0),(0,2),(2,0)\}.\)

The map that fixes 0 and 1 and sends 2 to 1 is a non-bijective endomorphism of _R_<sub>star</sub>. Therefore _R_<sub>star</sub> is not a core relation. Its image is {0,1}, and restricting the relation to this image gives CUT. Hence core(_R_<sub>star</sub>)=CUT on the core domain {0,1}.

The automorphisms of a core relation are the only unavoidable ambiguity when we try to force variables to chosen values. Let _X_ be a set of variables and let \(s:X\rightarrow D\) be a fixed assignment. We say that an _R_-instance _P<sub>s</sub> hard-pins s up to one common automorphism_ if it may use additional variables and

\(\{\alpha|_X:\alpha\in\mathrm{Sat}(P_s)\}=\{\sigma\circ s:\sigma\in\mathrm{Aut}(R)\}.\)

**Example 3.5.** For CUT, introduce two variables _y_<sub>0</sub>_,y_<sub>1</sub> and require CUT(_y_<sub>0</sub>_,y_<sub>1</sub>). If _s(x_)=0, add CUT(_x,y_<sub>1</sub>). If _s(x_)=1, add CUT(_x,y_<sub>0</sub>). These constraints force every \(x\in X\) to agree with _s_ after either the identity or the common swap of 0 and 1.

The relation _R_<sub>star</sub> above explains why we first reduce to a core. Its non-bijective endomorphism replaces the value 2 by 1. Applying this map to any satisfying assignment gives another satisfying assignment, so constraints over _R_<sub>star</sub> cannot in general distinguish these two values. After reducing _R_<sub>star</sub> to its core CUT, the construction above applies.

In Section 4.2, we prove that every core relation admits the same kind of construction.

## 3.5 Finite-domain degree

The parameter for Exact-CSP is the degree of the indicator function of the core relation. We define degree for any function \(f:D^k\rightarrow\mathbb{R}\). The domain _D_ need not contain a value already called 0. We choose any value of _D_ and call it 0. This choice only fixes the notation, and the reader may think of it as the usual value 0. For each coordinate \(i\in[k]\) and each \(a\in D\backslash\{0\}\), define _Z<sub>i,a</sub>(z_)=**1**\[_z<sub>i</sub>=a_\].

Every function \(f:D^k\rightarrow\mathbb{R}\) has a unique expansion<tbc>

\(f(z)=\sum_{T\subseteq[k]}\sum_{b\in(D\backslash\{0\})^T}\widehat{f}(T,b)\prod_{i\in T}Z_{i,b_i}(z),\)

where _b_ chooses one nonzero value _b<sub>i</sub>_ for every \(i\in T\). These products form a basis for all real-valued functions on _D<sup>k</sup>_. This follows by evaluating the function on points that are 0 outside _T_ and using inclusion-exclusion. In particular, when _f_ is integer-valued, all the coefficients \(\widehat{f}(T,b)\) are integers. We define deg_<sub>D</sub>(f_) to be the largest |_T_| for which \(\widehat{f}(T,b)\neq 0\), with constant functions having degree 0. Changing the basepoint changes the coefficients but not the degree. Indeed, the indicator of the old basepoint is one minus the sum of the indicators of all other values. Thus either set of indicators can be written using the other without increasing degree.

For a relation \(R\subseteq D^k\), we write **1**_<sub>R</sub>_ for its indicator function and use deg_<sub>D</sub>_(**1**_<sub>R</sub>_) as the degree of _R_.

**Example 3.6.** For CUT, let _Z<sub>i</sub>(z_)=**1**\[_z<sub>i</sub>_=1\]. Then

\(\mathbf{1}_\mathsf{CUT}(z_1,z_2)=Z_1(z)+Z_2(z)-2Z_1(z)Z_2(z),\)

so deg<sub>{0,1}</sub>(**1**<sub>CUT</sub>)=2.

As another example, let \(R_\mathsf{NAE}\subseteq\{0,1\}^3\) contain the tuples that are not constant. With _Z<sub>i</sub>(z_)=**1**\[_z<sub>i</sub>_=1\], we have

\(\mathbf{1}_{R_\mathsf{NAE}}(z)=Z_1(z)+Z_2(z)+Z_3(z)-Z_1(z)Z_2(z)-Z_1(z)Z_3(z)-Z_2(z)Z_3(z).\)

Thus deg<sub>{0,1}</sub>(**1**_<sub>R<sub>NAE</sub></sub>_)=2, even though _R_<sub>NAE</sub> has arity 3.

The upper and lower bounds for Exact-CSP will both use this degree after reducing the relation to its core.

### 3.6 Communication complexity

Our streaming lower bounds use the one-way communication problem INDEX_<sub>M</sub>_. Alice receives a string \(b\in\{0,1\}^M\), Bob receives an index \(i\in[M]\), and Bob must output _b<sub>i</sub>_. In a public-coin one-way protocol, Alice and Bob share a random string, Alice sends one message to Bob, and Bob produces the answer from this message, his index, and the shared randomness.

The connection to streaming is standard. Alice creates the first part of a stream from her input, runs the streaming algorithm on it, and sends the memory state to Bob. Bob resumes the algorithm from this state and appends constraints determined by his index. The memory state is the only message, so an _s_-space streaming algorithm gives a one-way protocol with _s_ bits of communication. The random tape of the streaming algorithm can be treated as the public random string.

We use the following standard lower bound.

**Lemma 3.7** (One-way complexity of INDEX, \[Abl96; KNR99\])**.** _Every randomized public-coin one-way protocol for_ INDEX_<sub>M</sub> with constant error uses_ \(\Omega(M)\) _bits of communication._

In each of our lower bounds, Alice’s part of the stream encodes her string, while Bob appends constraints that reveal the bit at his index. The rest of each reduction is devoted to constructing those constraints.

## 4 Properties of Cores

In this section, we prove the facts about cores that we will use throughout the paper. We first show that reducing to the core does not change any of our three objectives. We then give two ways to force an assignment using only constraints from a core relation. The first forces the assignment up<tbc>

<tbc>to one common automorphism and will be used for satisfiability. The second makes the same idea strong enough for exact optimization.

We will repeatedly use the fact that applying one automorphism to every assigned value changes nothing. We state it in the following observation.

**Observation 4.1.** _Let_ \(R\subseteq D^k\)_, let I be an R-instance, and let_ \(\sigma\in\mathrm{Aut}(R)\)_. For every assignment_ \(\alpha\)_, we have_ \(\mathrm{val}_I(\sigma\circ\alpha)=\mathrm{val}_I(\alpha)\)_. Therefore,_ \(\mathrm{unsatval}_I(\sigma\circ\alpha)=\mathrm{unsatval}_I(\alpha)\).

_Proof._ Consider a constraint _R(x_<sub>1</sub>_,...,x<sub>k</sub>_) of _I_. Since \(\sigma\) is an automorphism, the constraint is satisfied by \(\alpha\) if and only if it is satisfied by \(\sigma\circ\alpha\). This holds for every constraint, which proves both equalities.

## 4.1 Reduction to the core

The first goal is to reduce all three streaming problems from _R_ to its core _R<sup>⋆</sup>_. The reduction keeps every constraint on the same scope. It only replaces the relation _R_ by _R<sup>⋆</sup>_. The next lemma states that this preserves the streaming space exactly.

**Lemma 4.2.** _Let R<sup>⋆</sup>_=core(_R). The following statements hold._

(_i)_ SPACE(SAT(_R_))=SPACE(SAT(_R<sup>⋆</sup>_)).<tbc>

(_ii)_ _for every_ \(\gamma\ge 1\), \(\mathsf{SPACE}(\mathsf{Min}\mathsf{CSP}_\gamma(R))=\mathsf{SPACE}(\mathsf{Min}\mathsf{CSP}_\gamma(R^\star))\).<tbc>

_(iii)_ SPACE(Exact-CSP(_R_))=SPACE(Exact-CSP(_R<sup>⋆</sup>_)).

_The reductions preserve the number of variables and constraints, the scope of each corresponding constraint, stream order, and simplicity. If R is symmetric, then R<sup>⋆</sup> is symmetric as well._

To prove Lemma 4.2, we first prove that the same replacement preserves the two optimum values of every instance.

**Lemma 4.3.** _Let_ \(R\subseteq D^k\)_, let_ \(\sigma:D\rightarrow C\) _be an idempotent endomorphism of minimum image, and let_ \(R^\star=\mathrm{core}(R)=\sigma(R)=R\cap C^k\)_. Given an R-instance I, let I<sup>⋆</sup> be the R<sup>⋆</sup>-instance obtained by replacing every constraint R(x_<sub>1</sub>_,...,x<sub>k</sub>_) _by R<sup>⋆</sup>(x_<sub>1</sub>_,...,x<sub>k</sub>_) _on the same scope. Then_ OPT<sub>max</sub>(_I_)=OPT<sub>max</sub>(_I<sup>⋆</sup>_) _and_ OPT<sub>min</sub>(_I_)=OPT<sub>min</sub>(_I<sup>⋆</sup>). In particular, I is satisfiable if and only if I<sup>⋆</sup> is satisfiable._

_Proof._ Let \(\alpha\) be any assignment for _I_. If _R(x_<sub>1</sub>_,...,x<sub>k</sub>_) is satisfied by \(\alpha\), then \((\alpha(x_1),\dots,\alpha(x_k))\in R\), and applying the endomorphism \(\sigma\) gives \((\sigma(\alpha(x_1)),\dots,\sigma(\alpha(x_k)))\in\sigma(R)=R^\star\). Hence \(\mathrm{val}_{I^\star}(\sigma\circ\alpha)\ge\mathrm{val}_I(\alpha)\) and \(\mathrm{unsatval}_{I^\star}(\sigma\circ\alpha)\le\mathrm{unsatval}_I(\alpha)\). Taking an assignment that is optimal for the relevant objective gives \(\mathrm{OPT}_\mathrm{max}(I^\star)\ge\mathrm{OPT}_\mathrm{max}(I)\) and \(\mathrm{OPT}_\mathrm{min}(I^\star)\le\mathrm{OPT}_\mathrm{min}(I)\).

For the reverse direction, consider any assignment \(\beta\) taking values in _C_. Since \(R^\star=R\cap C^k\), every constraint is satisfied by \(\beta\) as an _R_-constraint if and only if it is satisfied by \(\beta\) as an _R<sup>⋆</sup>_-constraint. In particular, an assignment attaining either optimum for _I<sup>⋆</sup>_ is also an assignment for _I_ with the same value. Therefore \(\mathrm{OPT}_\mathrm{max}(I)\ge\mathrm{OPT}_\mathrm{max}(I^\star)\) and \(\mathrm{OPT}_\mathrm{min}(I)\le\mathrm{OPT}_\mathrm{min}(I^\star)\). Combining the two directions proves both equalities, and the satisfiability claim follows from OPT<sub>min</sub>=0.

We can now prove the streaming reduction. The point is that the instance level argument did not change any scope.

_Proof of Lemma 4.2._ Given a stream of _R_-constraints, replace each arriving constraint by the _R<sup>⋆</sup>_- constraint on the same scope and run an algorithm for _R<sup>⋆</sup>_. By Lemma 4.3, the final instance has the same two optimum values and is satisfiable exactly when the original instance is satisfiable. Conversely, replace every _R<sup>⋆</sup>_-constraint by the _R_-constraint on the same scope and use the same lemma again. Both transformations use only constant extra space and preserve the number of variables and constraints, the stream order, and simplicity. Finally, if _R_ is symmetric, then \(R^\star=R\cap C^k\) is symmetric as well.

Thus, from this point on, we may reduce to the core before proving any upper or lower bound.

## 4.2 Hard pinnings in a core relation

For the satisfiability lower bound, Bob will want to force the variables to a chosen witness assignment _s_. Ordinary _R_-constraints may not be able to distinguish _s_ from \(\sigma\circ s\) for an automorphism \(\sigma\), but this ambiguity is harmless by Observation 4.1. The next lemma shows that this is the only ambiguity we need to keep.

**Lemma 4.4** (Hard pinning)**.** _Let_ \(R\subseteq D^k\) _be a core relation, let X be a set of variables, and let_ \(s:X\rightarrow D\)_. There is an R-instance P<sub>s</sub> on X and O<sub>R</sub>_(1) _additional variables such that_

\(\{\alpha|_X:\alpha\in\mathrm{Sat}(P_s)\}=\{\sigma\circ s:\sigma\in\mathrm{Aut}(R)\}.\)

_Moreover, P<sub>s</sub> has O<sub>R</sub>_(|_X_|+1) _constraints._

The proof uses the following property of cores. Changing one domain value to another must make some tuple leave the relation.

**Lemma 4.5.** _Let_ \(R\subseteq D^k\) _be a core relation. For every distinct_ \(a,b\in D\)_, there is a tuple_ \(r=(r_1,\dots,r_k)\in R\) _and a coordinate_ \(t\in[k]\) _such that r<sub>t</sub>=a and_ \(r^{t\leftarrow b}\notin R\).

_Proof._ Define \(\sigma:D\rightarrow D\) by \(\sigma(a)=b\) and \(\sigma(c)=c\) for \(c\neq a\). The map \(\sigma\) is not injective, so it cannot be an endomorphism of the core relation _R_. Choose \(r\in R\) such that \(\sigma(r)\notin R\), and replace the occurrences of _a_ in _r_ by _b_ one at a time. The initial tuple is in _R_ and the final tuple is not, so at some first replacement we obtain a tuple outside _R_. Immediately before that replacement we have a tuple \(r'\in R\) with \(r'_t=a\), while \((r')^{t\leftarrow b}\notin R\). This is the required tuple.

We now build the hard-pinning instance. Intuitively, we introduce additional variables to represent the values of _D_, and a group of constraints forces their assigned values to form one automorphism of _R_.

_Proof of Lemma 4.4._ The first step is to introduce extra variables that represent the values in the domain, up to one common automorphism. For CUT, these are two adjacent variables, so they must receive opposite values. More formally, for every \(a\in D\), introduce an extra variable _y<sub>a</sub>_. For every tuple \(r=(r_1,\dots,r_k)\in R\), add the constraint _R(y_<sub>_r_<sub>1</sub></sub>_,...,y<sub>r<sub>k</sub></sub>_). Next, we add constraints that pin the variables in _X_ to _s_ up to the same automorphism. For every \(x\in X\), every \(r\in R\), and every \(t\in[k]\) with _r<sub>t</sub>=s(x_), also add _R(y_<sub>_r_<sub>1</sub></sub>_,...,y_<sub>_r<sub>t</sub>_-1</sub>_,x,y_<sub>_r<sub>t</sub>_+1</sub>_,...,y<sub>r<sub>k</sub></sub>_). Call the resulting instance _P<sub>s</sub>_. It uses |_D_|=_O<sub>R</sub>_(1) extra variables and _O<sub>R</sub>_(|_X_|+1) constraints.

We now prove that the added constraints give the required hard pinning. Let \(\alpha\) satisfy _P<sub>s</sub>_ and define \(\sigma:D\rightarrow D\) by \(\sigma(a)=\alpha(y_a)\). The first family of constraints shows that \(\sigma(r)\in R\) for every \(r\in R\), so \(\sigma\) is an endomorphism of _R_. Since _R_ is a core, \(\sigma\) is an automorphism. Fix \(x\in X\), put _a=s(x_), and let \(b=\sigma^{-1}(\alpha(x))\). Suppose \(b\neq a\). By Lemma 4.5, there are \(r\in R\) and \(t\in[k]\) such<tbc>

that _r<sub>t</sub>=a_ and \(r^{t\leftarrow b}\notin R\). The corresponding constraint from the second family is assigned the tuple \(\sigma(r^{t\leftarrow b})\), which is not in _R_ because \(\sigma\) is an automorphism. This contradicts that \(\alpha\) satisfies _P<sub>s</sub>_. Hence \(\alpha(x)=\sigma(s(x))\) for every \(x\in X\).

Conversely, fix any \(\sigma\in Aut(R)\) and assign \(y_a\mapsto\sigma(a)\) and \(x\mapsto\sigma(s(x))\). Every constraint in both families is then assigned a tuple of the form \(\sigma(r)\) for some \(r\in R\), so all constraints are satisfied. The restrictions of satisfying assignments to _X_ are therefore exactly the assignments \(\sigma\circ s\) with \(\sigma\in Aut(R)\).

The gadget therefore behaves like a genuine pinning whenever the objective is unchanged by a common automorphism. For exact optimization we need more because the goal is not merely to satisfy the whole instance. An assignment may gain constraints in the original instance by violating some constraints in the pinning gadget. We therefore need to ensure that deviating from the intended assignment loses more gadget constraints than it can gain in the original instance. We do this next.

## 4.3 Pinning for exact optimization

We now strengthen the construction for exact optimization. The input instance _P_ may reward an assignment for moving away from _s_, so a merely satisfiable pinning gadget is not enough. Intuitively, we replace each domain value by a block of many variables. The constraints among the blocks create a large loss unless their most frequent values form an automorphism, and the constraints joining _P_ to the blocks create a large loss whenever an original variable disagrees with _s_ under that automorphism.

**Lemma 4.6.** _Let_ \(R\subseteq D^k\) _be a core relation with_ \(k\ge 2\)_, and fix_ \(1\le d\le k\)_. Let P be a simple R-instance on O<sub>R</sub>(N_) _variables, with at most N<sup>d</sup> constraints and maximum variable degree at most N_<sup>_d_-1</sup>_. For every assignment s to the variables of P, there is an unweighted R-instance H<sub>s</sub>, using the variables of P and O<sub>R</sub>(N_) _additional variables, such that_ \(P\cup H_s\) _is simple and_

\(\mathrm{OPT}_{\mathrm{max}}(P\cup H_s)=|H_s|+\mathrm{val}_P(s).\)

_If R is symmetric and P has no repeated unordered scope, then_ \(P\cup H_s\) _has no repeated unordered scope. Moreover, H<sub>s</sub> can be constructed from R, the variable set of P, the assignment s, and the public parameters N and d. It does not depend on the constraints of P._

_Proof of Lemma 4.6._ Let _X_ be the variable set of _P_, let _B_ be the number of constraints in _P_, and let \(\Delta\) be its maximum variable degree. Thus \(B\le N^d\) and \(\Delta\le N^{d-1}\). We will choose a constant _C<sub>R</sub>_ below and set _m=C<sub>R</sub>N_.

The construction follows the same idea as Lemma 4.4. We first create many variables that represent each value of the domain up to one common automorphism. We then connect the variables of _P_ to these new variables. More formally, for every \(a\in D\), create a _block Z<sub>a</sub>_ of _m_ new variables. For every tuple \(r=(r_1,\dots,r_k)\in R\) and every choice of pairwise distinct variables \(z_i\in Z_{r_i}\), add the constraint _R(z_<sub>1</sub>_,...,z<sub>k</sub>_). We call these the _block constraints_. Next fix \(x\in X\) and put _a=s(x_). For every \(r\in R\), every \(t\in[k]\) with _r<sub>t</sub>=a_, and every choice of pairwise distinct variables \(z_j\in Z_{r_j}\) for \(j\neq t\), add the constraint _R(z_<sub>1</sub>_,...,z_<sub>_t_-1</sub>_,x,z_<sub>_t_+1</sub>_,...,z<sub>k</sub>_). We call these the _attached constraints for x_. If the same ordered scope arises more than once, keep only one constraint. When _R_ is symmetric, keep only one constraint for each unordered scope. Let _H<sub>s</sub>_ be the union of the block constraints and all the attached constraints.

Firstly note that the instance \(P\cup H_s\) is simple. This is because the constraints of _P_ use only variables in _X_, block constraints use only variables from the blocks, and an attached constraint for<tbc>

<tbc>_x_ uses _x_ together with _k_-1 variables from the blocks. The removal of duplicate scopes makes each family simple, and attached constraints for two different variables of _X_ cannot have the same scope. The number of new variables is |_D|m=O<sub>R</sub>(N_). This construction uses the variable set of _P_ but not its constraints, as required in the final part of the lemma.

We next show the counting bound that we need. Let _q_=|_D_|. Under any assignment \(\alpha\), choose a most frequent value in each block _Z<sub>a</sub>_ and denote it by \(\sigma(a)\). This value appears at least _m/q_ times in _Z<sub>a</sub>_. Consider any sequence of \(\ell\le k\) blocks and choose one variable from each block in order. At every step, at most _k_-1 variables are forbidden by the earlier choices. Hence, when \(m\ge 2qk\), there are at least _m/_(2_q_) choices at every step and at least \((m/(2q))^\ell\) pairwise distinct choices in total. At most _k_! ordered choices give the same unordered scope. We may therefore fix a constant \(\eta_R>0\) such that there are at least \(\eta_Rm^\ell\) distinct ordered scopes, and also at least \(\eta_Rm^\ell\) distinct unordered scopes when _R_ is symmetric. For a fixed tuple _r_, different ordered choices give different ordered scopes of block constraints. The same is true for the attached constraints when _x_, _r_, and _t_ are fixed. Thus the bound continues to hold after we remove repeated scopes.

Choose _C<sub>R</sub>_ large enough that \(C_R\ge 2qk\), \(\eta_RC_R^k>1\), and \(\eta_RC_R^{k-1}>1\). Since _m=C<sub>R</sub>N_, \(B\le N^d\), \(\Delta\le N^{d-1}\), and \(d\le k\), we then have \(\eta_Rm^k>B\) and \(\eta_Rm^{k-1}>\Delta\) for every \(N\ge 1\).

We can now compare every assignment with the intended one. Assigning \(x\mapsto s(x)\) for \(x\in X\) and assigning every variable in _Z<sub>a</sub>_ the value _a_ satisfies all constraints of _H<sub>s</sub>_. Therefore \(\mathrm{OPT}_\mathrm{max}(P\cup H_s)\ge|H_s|+\mathrm{val}_P(s)\).

For the reverse inequality, fix an arbitrary assignment \(\alpha\) and define \(\sigma:D\rightarrow D\) from the most frequent values of the blocks as above. Suppose first that \(\sigma\) is not an endomorphism of _R_. Choose \(r\in R\) with \(\sigma(r)\notin R\). At least \(\eta_Rm^k>B\) block constraints are assigned the tuple \(\sigma(r)\), so all of them are violated. Even if \(\alpha\) satisfies every constraint of _P_, it has value less than |_H<sub>s</sub>_|, while the intended assignment has value at least |_H<sub>s</sub>_|. Thus any assignment that attains the optimum must have \(\sigma\) as an endomorphism and, since _R_ is a core, as an automorphism.

Thus, we only need to consider the case in which \(\sigma\) is an automorphism. Let \(W=\{x\in X:\alpha(x)\neq\sigma(s(x))\}\). Fix \(x\in W\), put _a=s(x_), and put \(b=\sigma^{-1}(\alpha(x))\), so \(b\neq a\). By Lemma 4.5, there are \(r\in R\) and \(t\in[k]\) such that _r<sub>t</sub>=a_ and \(r^{t\leftarrow b}\notin R\). In every other coordinate _j_, choose a variable from _Z<sub>r<sub>j</sub></sub>_ assigned its most frequent value \(\sigma(r_j)\). There are at least \(\eta_Rm^{k-1}\) such attached constraints for _x_, and each is assigned the tuple \(\sigma(r^{t\leftarrow b})\). All of them are violated because \(\sigma\) is an automorphism. The constraints counted for different variables _x_ are disjoint, so \(\alpha\) violates at least \(\eta_Rm^{k-1}|W|\) attached constraints.

The assignment \(\sigma\circ s\) has value val_<sub>P</sub>(s_) on _P_ by Observation 4.1. Changing the variables in _W_ can affect at most \(\Delta|W|\) constraints of _P_, and hence \(\mathrm{val}_P(\alpha|_X)\le\mathrm{val}_P(s)+\Delta|W|\). Since \(\alpha\) violates at least \(\eta_Rm^{k-1}|W|\) attached constraints, we have \(\mathrm{val}_{P\cup H_s}(\alpha)\le|H_s|+\mathrm{val}_P(s)+(\Delta-\eta_Rm^{k-1})|W|\le|H_s|+\mathrm{val}_P(s)\). Together with the intended assignment, this proves the required equality.

The exact-pinning gadget still leaves one common automorphism, but that is fine since the objective of _P_ is invariant under it, while every other disagreement with _s_ loses more gadget constraints than it can gain in _P_.

## 5 Satisfability

We now characterize the one-pass streaming space needed to decide satisfiability. We will prove that after reducing to the core, the right parameter is non-redundancy. The upper bound stores a small instance with the same satisfying assignments as the constraints seen so far. For the lower bound, a maximum nonredundant instance gives the bits of an INDEX instance, and hard pinning lets Bob test the bit corresponding to his constraint.

**Theorem 5.1** (Satisfiability)**.** _Let_ \(R\subseteq D^k\) _be a fixed non-trivial relation and let R<sup>⋆</sup>_=core(_R). The following statements hold._

(_i)_ _there is a deterministic one-pass streaming algorithm for_ SAT(_R_) _using O<sub>R</sub>_(NRD_<sub>n</sub>(R<sup>⋆</sup>_)log_n_) _bits of space._<tbc>

_(ii)_ _every randomized bounded-error one-pass streaming algorithm for_ SAT(_R_) _uses_ \(\Omega_R(\mathsf{NRD}_n(R^\star))\) _bits of space._

_Consequently,_

\(\Omega_R(\mathsf{NRD}_n(\mathsf{core}(R)))\le\mathsf{SPACE}(\mathsf{SAT}(R))\le O_R(\mathsf{NRD}_n(\mathsf{core}(R))\mathrm{log}n).\)

We prove the two bounds for a core relation and then use Lemma 4.2 to obtain the theorem for an arbitrary relation.

The upper bound is the following known consequence of non-redundancy \[SV26a, Theorem 1(a)\].

**Lemma 5.2** (Satisfiability upper bound)**.** _\[SV26a, Theorem 1(a)\] If R is a core relation, then_ SAT(_R_) _has a deterministic one-pass streaming algorithm using O<sub>R</sub>_(NRD_<sub>n</sub>(R_)log_n_) _bits of space._

The algorithm maintains a nonredundant subinstance with exactly the same satisfying assignments as the current prefix of the stream. When a constraint arrives, the algorithm adds it and repeatedly removes any constraint whose deletion does not change the set of satisfying assignments. The stored instance therefore has at most NRD_<sub>n</sub>(R_) constraints. Since _R_ is fixed, each constraint is specified by its scope using _O<sub>R</sub>_(log_n_) bits. There is no update-time restriction, so redundancy and final satisfiability can be checked by trying all assignments using _O<sub>R</sub>(n_) additional bits. For a non-trivial relation, \(\mathsf{NRD}_n(R)=\Omega_R(n)\), so this is within the stated space bound. For a trivial relation, satisfiability is immediate.

It remains to prove the matching lower bound. The reduction uses the witnesses of a nonredundant instance in the way suggested by the definition of non-redundancy.

## 5.1 Lower bound for a core relation

In this subsection, we prove the following main theorem.

**Theorem 5.3** (Satisfiability lower bound)**.** _Let_ \(R\subseteq D^k\) _be a core relation. Every randomized bounded-error one-pass streaming algorithm for_ SAT(_R_) _uses_ \(\Omega_R(\mathsf{NRD}_n(R))\) _bits of space._

_Proof._ The idea is simple. Alice streams a subinstance of a maximum nonredundant instance. Bob takes the witness for his queried constraint, meaning an assignment that violates this constraint and satisfies every other constraint in the nonredundant instance, and uses Lemma 4.4 to force that witness up to one automorphism. Since automorphisms preserve which constraints are satisfied, the resulting instance tells Bob whether Alice streamed the queried constraint.

Let _c<sub>R</sub>_ be a constant such that the hard-pinning instance in Lemma 4.4 always uses at most _c<sub>R</sub>_ additional variables. Fix a sufficiently large number _n_, put _n_<sub>0</sub>=_n-c<sub>R</sub>_, and let _F_={_C_<sub>1</sub>_,...,C<sub>M</sub>_} be a nonredundant _R_-instance on _n_<sub>0</sub> variables with _M_=NRD<sub>_n_<sub>0</sub></sub>(_R_). If _M_=0, the claimed lower bound is empty, so assume \(M\ge 1\). For every \(i\in[M]\), choose a witness assignment _s<sub>i</sub>_ that violates _C<sub>i</sub>_ and satisfies every _C<sub>j</sub>_ with \(j\neq i\).

Suppose that a randomized one-pass streaming algorithm decides SAT(_R_) on _n_ variables using _S(n_) bits of space. We use it to solve INDEX_<sub>M</sub>_. Alice receives a string \(x\in\{0,1\}^M\), and Bob receives an index \(i\in[M]\). Alice starts the streaming algorithm and streams _C<sub>j</sub>_ exactly when _x<sub>j</sub>_=1. She<tbc>

<tbc>then sends the _S(n_)-bit memory state to Bob. Bob resumes the algorithm from this state and appends the hard-pinning instance _P<sub>s<sub>i</sub></sub>_ from Lemma 4.4. The final instance uses at most _n_<sub>0</sub>+_c<sub>R</sub>=n_ variables.

We claim that the final instance is satisfiable if and only if _x<sub>i</sub>_=0. Suppose first that _x<sub>i</sub>_=0. The assignment _s<sub>i</sub>_ satisfies every constraint streamed by Alice, and it extends to a satisfying assignment of _P<sub>s<sub>i</sub></sub>_ by using the identity automorphism in Lemma 4.4. Hence the final instance is satisfiable.

Now suppose that _x<sub>i</sub>_=1. Any assignment satisfying _P<sub>s<sub>i</sub></sub>_ restricts on the original variables to \(\sigma\circ s_i\) for some \(\sigma\in\mathrm{Aut}(R)\). The assignment _s<sub>i</sub>_ violates _C<sub>i</sub>_, so Observation 4.1 implies that \(\sigma\circ s_i\) also violates _C<sub>i</sub>_. Since Alice streamed _C<sub>i</sub>_, no assignment can satisfy the final instance. This proves the claim.

Alice and Bob use the random tape of the streaming algorithm as public randomness. Bob outputs the complement of the algorithm’s answer, which recovers _x<sub>i</sub>_ with the same constant error probability. We have therefore obtained a public-coin one-way protocol for INDEX_<sub>M</sub>_ with _S(n_) bits of communication. By Lemma 3.7, \(S(n)=\Omega(M)=\Omega(\mathsf{NRD}_{n_0}(R))\).

Finally, we need to prove that removing a constant number of variables changes non-redundancy by at most a constant factor depending only on _R_. We start with a maximum nonredundant instance on at most _n_ variables and add unused variables so that its variable set has size exactly _n_. Choose a uniformly random set of _n_<sub>0</sub>=_n-c<sub>R</sub>_ variables. A constraint uses at most _k_ distinct variables, so for all sufficiently large _n_ the probability that all variables in its scope are chosen is bounded below by a positive constant dependent only on _R_. Some choice therefore keeps \(\Omega_R(\mathsf{NRD}_n(R))\) constraints. These constraints remain nonredundant because their original witnesses can be restricted to the chosen variables. Thus \(\mathsf{NRD}_{n_0}(R)=\Omega_R(\mathsf{NRD}_n(R))\), and consequently \(S(n)=\Omega_R(\mathsf{NRD}_n(R))\).

We now combine the core reduction with the two core relation bounds to conclude the proof of Theorem 5.1.

_Proof of Theorem 5.1._ By Lemma 4.2, deciding SAT(_R_) has the same streaming space complexity as deciding SAT(_R<sup>⋆</sup>_). Apply Lemma 5.2 to _R<sup>⋆</sup>_ for the deterministic upper bound and Theorem 5.3 to _R<sup>⋆</sup>_ for the randomized lower bound. This gives both parts of the theorem and the claimed characterization.

Thus the streaming complexity of satisfiability is governed, up to the logarithmic factor in the upper bound, by the non-redundancy of the core relation.

## 6 Sparsification and Min-CSP

We first state our sparsification result for CSPs that are revealed in streams.

**Theorem 6.1** (Sparsification)**.** _Let_ \(R\subseteq D^k\) _be a fixed non-trivial relation and let_ \(\varepsilon>0\)_. There is a deterministic one-pass streaming algorithm which, given an unweighted stream of constraints defining an R-instance I on n variables and with stream length m, stores a weighted subinstance_ \(H\subseteq I\) _such that for every assignment_ \(\alpha\), \(\mathrm{unsatval}_H(\alpha)\in(1\pm\varepsilon)\mathrm{unsatval}_I(\alpha)\)_. The space used is_ \(O_{R,\varepsilon}(\mathsf{NRD}_n(R)\cdot\mathrm{polylog}(n,m,1/\varepsilon))\).

As an immediate corollary, we obtain the following.

**Corollary 6.2** (Min-CSP)**.** _Let_ \(R\subseteq D^k\) _be a fixed non-trivial relation, let R<sup>⋆</sup>_=core(_R), and let_ \(\varepsilon>0\).

(_i)_ _there is a deterministic one-pass_ \((1+\varepsilon)\)_-approximation algorithm for_ Min-CSP(_R_) _using_ \(O_{R,\varepsilon}(\mathsf{NRD}_n(R^\star)\mathrm{polylog}(n,m,1/\varepsilon))\) _bits of space;_<tbc>

_(ii)_ _every randomized bounded-error one-pass finite-factor approximation algorithm for_ Min-CSP(_R_) _uses_ \(\Omega_R(\mathsf{NRD}_n(R^\star))\) _bits._

_Consequently,_

\(\Omega_R(\mathsf{NRD}_n(\mathrm{core}(R)))\le\mathsf{SPACE}(\mathsf{Min}-\mathsf{CSP}_{1+\varepsilon}(R))\le O_{R,\varepsilon}(\mathsf{NRD}_n(\mathrm{core}(R))\mathrm{polylog}(n,m,1/\varepsilon)).\)

We first prove Theorem 6.1. The proof of Corollary 6.2 is given at the end of the section.

## 6.1 Sparsification

At a high level, we use a sparsify-merge-sparsify procedure for building sparsifiers in insertion-only streams. These sparsifiers have been used before in insertion-only streams; see, for instance, \[McG14\]. The only sparsification result we need as a black box is the following theorem of Brakensiek and Guruswami.

**Fact 6.3** (\[BG25\])**.** _If_ \(\mathcal{C}\subseteq\{0,1\}^M\) _is a binary code and_ \(0<\eta<1\)_, then there is a nonnegative weight vector z such that_<tbc>

\(\langle z,c\rangle\in(1\pm\eta)\|c\|_1\text{\textit{for every}}c\in\mathcal{C},\)

<tbc>_and, for an absolute constant c_<sub>BG</sub>_\>_0,

\(|\mathrm{supp}(z)|\le c_\mathrm{BG}\mathsf{NRD}(\mathcal{C})\frac{\mathrm{log}_2^6(4M)}{\eta^2}.\) (6.4)

_Importantly, their proof allows z to be chosen with nonnegative integer entries. Indeed, their induction starts with unit weights and, in the recursive step, assigns weight_ 1 _to the explicitly retained coordinates and multiplies the recursively produced weights by_ 3.

Subsequent work sharpened and broadened this code-sparsification framework. Lovett, Meka, and Wang \[LMW26\] improved the dependence on the block length from polylogarithmic to logarithmic, while Khanna, Putterman, and Sudan \[KPS26\] developed a unified sparsification theory for nonnegative real-valued codes.

Note that in the above, NRD(C) refers to the largest _identity_ submatrix that can be found in C (when its vectors are listed as rows).

We now prove the following basic fact which shows that weighted instances (with small weights) can effectively be sparsified as _unweighted_ instances, just by repeating constraints.

**Lemma 6.5** (Integral-weight reduction)**.** _Let J be an integer-weighted R-instance on at most n variables. Let_<tbc>

\(W(J)=\sum_{C\in\mathrm{supp}(J)}w_J(C),\)

<tbc>_denote the total weight of the instance. For every_ \(0<\eta<1\)_, there is an integer-weighted subinstance_ \(\mathrm{Red}_\eta(J)\subseteq J\) _such that, simultaneously for every assignment_ \(\alpha\),

\(\mathrm{unsatval}_{\mathrm{Red}_\eta(J)}(\alpha)\in(1\pm\eta)\mathrm{unsatval}_J(\alpha),\) (6.6)

_and_

\(|\mathrm{supp}(\mathrm{Red}_\eta(J))|\le c_\mathrm{BG}\mathsf{NRD}_n(R)\frac{\mathrm{log}_2^6(4\mathrm{max}\{W(J),1\})}{\eta^2}.\) (6.7)

_Proof._ The assertion is immediate when _W(J_)=0, so assume _W(J)\>_0. Because the instance is integer weighted, we simply replace each constraint _C_ of weight _w<sub>J</sub>(C_) by _w<sub>J</sub>(C_) labeled unit-weight copies. Denote the resulting unweighted multiset by \(J^\unknown\); it has exactly _W(J_) occurrences. Now, for this _unweighted_ CSP instance, we construct the canonical "violation code".

\(\mathcal{C}_{J^\unknown}=\left\{\big(\mathbf{1}[\alpha\text{violates}C]\big)_{C\in J^\unknown}:\alpha:V(J)\rightarrow D\right\}\subseteq\{0,1\}^{W(J)}.\) (6.8)

We claim that

\(\mathsf{NRD}(\mathcal{C}_{J^\unknown})\le\mathsf{NRD}_n(R).\) (6.9)

Indeed, suppose that _t_ coordinates form an identity submatrix, and let _C_<sub>1</sub>_,...,C<sub>t</sub>_ be the corresponding constraint copies. For every \(i\in[t]\), the row containing the _i_th diagonal 1 is an assignment that violates _C<sub>i</sub>_ and satisfies every _C<sub>j</sub>_ with \(j\neq i\). Hence {_C_<sub>1</sub>_,...,C<sub>t</sub>_} is a nonredundant _R_-instance on at most _n_ variables. Notice also that two copies of the same constraint, or two distinct constraints operating on the same ordered tuple of variables, have identical columns and therefore cannot both appear in such an identity submatrix.

Next, we apply (6.4) to \(\mathcal{C}_{J^\unknown}\). Its integer weight vector approximately preserves the number of violated copies for every assignment. To build the ultimate sparsifier, we collapse all selected copies belonging to the same occurrence of _J_ and add their weights. Since we impose no restriction on computation time, the required weight vector can be found deterministically within the stated space bound by enumerating candidate supports and integer weights and checking the inequalities over all assignments. Coordinates that are identically zero may be discarded, while every remaining selected weight is at most \((1+\eta)W(J)\), so this search is finite. This then yields (6.6) and (6.7).

Now, we proceed to give the streaming construction. It is enough to consider an ultimate sparsifier accuracy of \(0<\varepsilon\le 1/2\). For a larger error, run the construction with error 1/2. We then set

\(\eta_\ell=\frac{\varepsilon}{20(\ell+1)^2}(\ell\ge 1).\) (6.10)

The algorithm maintains at most one sparsifier at each level \(\ell\ge 0\). A level-\(\ell\) sparsifier represents a block of exactly \(2^\ell\) original constraints in the stream. Whenever the algorithm stores two sparsifiers at level \(\ell\), we take their weighted union _J_ and replace it by

\(\mathrm{Red}_{\eta_{\ell+1}}(J),\)

which now constitutes a sparsifier at level \(\ell+1\). We repeat this carry operation until every level again contains at most one sparsifier.

**Claim 6.11.** _Let H<sub>B</sub> be a level-_\(\ell\) _sparsifier and let I<sub>B</sub> be the unweighted subinstance consisting of its underlying block of constraints. Then, for every assignment_ \(\alpha\),

\(\left(\prod_{j=1}^\ell(1-\eta_j)\right)\mathrm{unsatval}_{I_B}(\alpha)\le\mathrm{unsatval}_{H_B}(\alpha)\le\left(\prod_{j=1}^\ell(1+\eta_j)\right)\mathrm{unsatval}_{I_B}(\alpha).\) (6.12)

_Consequently, the union of the sparsifiers remaining at the end of the stream is a_ \((1\pm\varepsilon)\)_-sparsifier of the entire input._

_Proof._ We prove (6.12) by induction on \(\ell\). It is an equality at level zero. Suppose two level-\((\ell-1)\) sparsifiers _H_<sub>_B_<sub>1</sub></sub> and _H_<sub>_B_<sub>2</sub></sub> are merged. Since all values are nonnegative, adding their two inductive inequalities shows that their weighted union has the same multiplicative bounds relative to \(I_{B_1}\unknown I_{B_2}\).

Applying \(\mathrm{Red}_{\eta_\ell}\) multiplies the lower and upper bounds by \(1-\eta_\ell\) and \(1+\eta_\ell\), respectively, thereby yielding the induction.

The schedule satisfies<tbc>

\(s:=\sum_{\ell\ge 1}\eta_\ell<\frac{\varepsilon}{20}\le\frac{1}{40}.\)

<tbc>Therefore<tbc>

\(\prod_{\ell\ge 1}(1-\eta_\ell)\ge 1-s\ge 1-\varepsilon\)

<tbc>and, using \(e^x\le 1+2x\) for \(0\le x\le 1/2\),

\(\prod_{\ell\ge 1}(1+\eta_\ell)\le e^s\le 1+2s\le 1+\varepsilon.\)

This then finishes the claim.

**Claim 6.13.** _Let d_=NRD_<sub>n</sub>(R). A level-_\(\ell\) _sparsifier has support size at most_

\(O_R\big(\frac{d}{\varepsilon^2}(\ell+1)^{10}\big),\) (6.14)

_and each of its positive weights is an integer smaller than_ \(2^{\ell+1}\)_. On a stream of length m, the total space used is bounded by_

_bits._

\(b_\ell=\prod_{j=1}^\ell(1+\eta_j).\)

\(q^{-k}W(H_B)\le\mathbb{E}_\unknown[\mathrm{unsatval}_{H_B}(\unknown)]\le b_\ell\mathbb{E}_\unknown[\mathrm{unsatval}_{I_B}(\unknown)]<2^{\ell+1}.\)
