## 7 Exact-CSP

We now determine the one-pass streaming space needed to solve Exact-CSP(_R_) on simple instances. As in the previous sections, we first reduce _R_ to its core. After this reduction, the answer is governed by the degree of the core relation.

The two bounds use degree in different ways. For the upper bound, the degree-_d_ representation of **1**_<sub>R</sub>_ lets us write the number of satisfied constraints using only terms that involve at most _d_ variables. The algorithm keeps the coefficient of each such term. When \(d\ge 1\), the lower bound uses 2_<sup>d</sup>_ assignments and a signed sum of their values that isolates one chosen constraint. The construction in Lemma 4.6 then lets Bob recover each of these values from the exact optimum returned by the streaming algorithm.

**Theorem 7.1** (Exact-CSP)**.** _Let_ \(R\subseteq D^k\)_, let R<sup>⋆</sup>_=core(_R_) _have core domain C, and put d_=deg_<sub>C</sub>_(**1**_<sub>R<sup>⋆</sup></sub>). The following statements hold._

(_i)_ _There is a deterministic one-pass algorithm for_ Exact-CSP(_R_) _using O<sub>R</sub>(n<sup>d</sup>_log(_n_+1)) _bits on unweighted simple instances._<tbc>

(_ii)_ _If_ \(d\ge 1\)_, every randomized bounded-error one-pass algorithm for_ Exact-CSP(_R_) _on unweighted simple instances uses_ \(\Omega_R(n^d)\) _bits of space._<tbc>

_(iii)_ _If R is symmetric and_ \(d\ge 1\)_, the lower bound holds even when no unordered scope is repeated._

_Consequently, when_ \(d\ge 1\),

\(\Omega_R(n^d)\le\mathsf{SPACE}(\mathsf{Exact-CSP}(R))\le O_R(n^dlog(n+1)).\)

_When d_=0_, the relation R<sup>⋆</sup> is either empty or equal to C<sup>k</sup>. Thus the optimum is either always_ 0 _or is the number of constraints in the stream, and it can be found using O<sub>R</sub>_(log(_n_+1)) _bits on simple instances._

We prove the upper bound directly. We then prove the lower bound for a core relation and use Lemma 4.2 to obtain the result for an arbitrary relation.

The upper bound follows by keeping the coefficients of a low-degree representation of the objective. The Boolean version of this argument appears in \[KPSY23, Section 1.1\]. We give a generalization of their result to any finite domain.

**Lemma 7.2** (Exact-CSP upper bound)**.** _Let_ \(R\subseteq D^k\)_, let R<sup>⋆</sup>_=core(_R_) _have core domain C, and put d_=deg_<sub>C</sub>_(**1**_<sub>R<sup>⋆</sup></sub>). There is a deterministic one-pass algorithm that solves_ Exact-CSP(_R_) _on an instance with n variables and m constraints using O<sub>R</sub>(n<sup>d</sup>_(log(_n_+1)+log(_m_+1))) _bits of space. In particular, on simple instances the space is O<sub>R</sub>(n<sup>d</sup>_log(_n_+1)).

_Proof._ By Lemma 4.2, we may replace each arriving _R_-constraint by the _R<sup>⋆</sup>_-constraint on the same scope. We will describe a small representation of the value of every assignment for this _R<sup>⋆</sup>_-instance.

Fix a basepoint \(0\in C\). For a variable _x_ and a value \(a\in C\backslash\{0\}\), define the indicator \(X_{x,a}(\alpha)=\mathbf{1}[\alpha(x)=a]\). This indicator is 1 exactly when \(\alpha\) gives _x_ the value _a_, and it is 0 otherwise. By the definition of _d_=deg_<sub>C</sub>_(**1**_<sub>R<sup>⋆</sup></sub>_), membership in _R<sup>⋆</sup>_ can be written as a polynomial in the indicators of coordinate values, with every monomial involving at most _d_ coordinates. In other words, there are constants _c<sub>T,b</sub>_ such that, for every \(z=(z_1,\dots,z_k)\in C^k\),

\(\mathbf{1}_{R^\star}(z)=\sum_{T\subseteq[k]|T|\le d}\sum_{b\in(C\backslash\{0\})^T}c_{T,b}\prod_{j\in T}\mathbf{1}[z_j=b_j].\)

The relation is fixed, so this sum has _O<sub>R</sub>_(1) terms and all the constants _c<sub>T,b</sub>_ depend only on _R_. They are integers by the inclusion-exclusion description of the coefficients in Section 3.5.

Consider an arriving constraint _R<sup>⋆</sup>(x_<sub>_i_<sub>1</sub></sub>_,...,x<sub>i<sub>k</sub></sub>_). For this constraint, set \(z_j=\alpha(x_{i_j})\) for every \(j\in[k]\) in the formula above. We obtain

\(\mathbf{1}[R^\star(x_{i_1},\dots,x_{i_k})\text{is satisfied by}\alpha]=\sum_{T\subseteq[k]|T|\le d}\sum_{b\in(C\backslash\{0\})^T}c_{T,b}\prod_{j\in T}X_{x_{i_j},b_j}(\alpha).\)

This formula expresses whether \(\alpha\) satisfies this constraint as a sum of products of the indicators _X<sub>x,a</sub>_. Each product checks the values of at most _d_ variables from the scope. If the same variable appears twice in a product with the same required value, the two identical indicators can be replaced by one. If it appears with two different required values, no assignment can make both indicators equal to 1, so the product is always zero and can be omitted.

The algorithm keeps one integer counter for every product of the form \(\prod_{x\in U}X_{x,a_x}\) with \(|U|\le d\). When a constraint arrives, the algorithm writes its satisfaction indicator using the formula above and adds each _c<sub>T,b</sub>_ to the counter for the corresponding product. There are at most \(\sum_{j=0}^d\genfrac(){pt}{2}{n}{j}(|C|-1)^j=O_R(n^d)\) possible products. Each counter has magnitude _O<sub>R</sub>(m_) and therefore uses _O<sub>R</sub>_(log(_m_+1)) bits. Identifying its variables and values uses _O<sub>R</sub>_(log(_n_+1)) bits. The total space is _O<sub>R</sub>(n<sup>d</sup>_(log(_n_+1)+log(_m_+1))).

After the stream, the sum of the stored terms is exactly \(\mathrm{val}_{I^\star}(\alpha)\) for every assignment \(\alpha\), where _I<sup>⋆</sup>_ is the resulting _R<sup>⋆</sup>_-instance. The algorithm can try all assignments, evaluate this sum, and return its maximum. There is no restriction on the time used after the stream. By Lemma 4.3, this maximum is also OPT<sub>max</sub>(_I_) for the original _R_-instance _I_. Finally, a simple instance has at most _n<sup>k</sup>_ constraints, so log(_m_+1)=_O<sub>R</sub>_(log(_n_+1)).

This proves the upper bound in Theorem 7.1, including the case _d_=0. We now assume \(d\ge 1\) and prove the lower bound.

## 7.1 Lower bound for a core relation

We first prove the lower bound when _R_ is already a core. This is the main result of the subsection.

**Theorem 7.3** (Lower bound for Exact-CSP on a core relation)**.** _Let_ \(R\subseteq D^k\) _be a core relation and let_ \(d=\mathrm{deg}_D(\mathbf{1}_R)\ge 1\)_. Every randomized bounded-error one-pass algorithm for_ Exact-CSP(_R_) _on unweighted simple instances uses_ \(\Omega_R(n^d)\) _bits of space. If R is symmetric, the statement holds with unordered simplicity._

The proof is a reduction from INDEX<sub>_N<sup>d</sup>_</sub>. Alice will associate one constraint with each vector in \[_N_\]_<sup>d</sup>_ and stream that constraint exactly when the corresponding bit is 1. Bob must determine whether Alice streamed one chosen constraint. To do this, he will consider 2_<sup>d</sup>_ assignments and add or subtract their values. The next lemma shows that these signs can be chosen so that the selected constraint has a nonzero total contribution. Later, we will arrange that every other constraint has total contribution zero.

More precisely, each of the _d_ relevant coordinates will take either a basepoint 0 or one fixed value _a<sub>i</sub>_. The assignments are indexed by the sets \(S\subseteq[d]\) of coordinates that receive _a<sub>i</sub>_. The expression in the next lemma is simply the value on these 2_<sup>d</sup>_ choices, added with a plus sign when _d_-|_S_| is even and a minus sign when it is odd.

**Lemma 7.4.** _Let_ \(R\subseteq D^k\) _and suppose_ \(\mathrm{deg}_D(\mathbf{1}_R)=d\ge 1\)_. Fix any basepoint_ \(0\in D\)_. Then there are distinct coordinates_ \(t_1,\dots,t_d\in[k]\) _and values_ \(a_1,\dots,a_d\in D\backslash\{0\}\) _such that, after fixing every coordinate outside_ {_t_<sub>1</sub>_,...,t<sub>d</sub>_} _to_ 0_, the resulting function_ \(h:D^d\rightarrow\{0,1\}\) _satisfies_

\(c:=\sum_{S\subseteq[d]}(-1)^{d-|S|}h(y^S)\neq 0,\)

_where_ \(y_i^S=a_i\) _for_ \(i\in S\) _and_ \(y_i^S=0\) _otherwise._

_Proof._ For \(j\in[k]\) and \(a\in D\backslash\{0\}\), define _Z<sub>j,a</sub>(x_)=**1**\[_x<sub>j</sub>=a_\]. As in the upper bound, the definition of degree gives an expansion

\(\mathbf{1}_R(x)=\sum_{T\subseteq[k]}\sum_{b\in(D\backslash\{0\})^T}c_{T,b}\prod_{j\in T}Z_{j,b_j}(x).\)

Since the degree is _d_, there is a set _T_={_t_<sub>1</sub>_,...,t<sub>d</sub>_} and a choice of values \(a_1,\dots,a_d\in D\backslash\{0\}\) for which the coefficient _c<sub>T,a</sub>_ is nonzero. Fix every coordinate outside _T_ to 0. Any term involving one of those coordinates is now zero because all the indicators in the expansion correspond to nonzero values.

Consider the signed sum in the statement one term of the expansion at a time. If a term does not use coordinate _t<sub>i</sub>_, then its value is unchanged when _i_ is added to or removed from _S_. The sets _S_ and \(S\triangleup\{i\}\) have opposite signs, so their contributions cancel. Therefore, only terms that use all _d_ coordinates in _T_ can remain. There are no terms of degree larger than _d_, and among the degree-_d_ terms on _T_, only the term requiring the values _a_<sub>1</sub>_,...,a<sub>d</sub>_ is nonzero on the chosen 2_<sup>d</sup>_ tuples. Its total contribution is its coefficient _c<sub>T,a</sub>_. Hence the number _c_ in the statement equals _c<sub>T,a</sub>_ and is nonzero.

We now use these 2_<sup>d</sup>_ choices in the reduction. The queried constraint will see all of them and will therefore contribute _c_. Any other constraint will be unaffected by at least one of the choices. Pairing the two assignments that differ only in that choice will make its contribution cancel.

_Proof of Theorem 7.3._ Without loss of generality, we may assume that the coordinates _t_<sub>1</sub>_,...,t<sub>d</sub>_ from Lemma 7.4 are the first _d_ coordinates. This is because if they are not, we can permute the coordinates of _R_ and apply the same permutation to every scope without changing the streaming problem. Fix the values _a_<sub>1</sub>_,...,a<sub>d</sub>_ and the nonzero integer _c_ given by that lemma. If _k_=1 and |_D|\>_1, a unary relation always has a non-bijective endomorphism. For a nonempty relation, use a constant map to a value in the relation. For the empty relation, use any non-bijective map. Thus a unary core relation has a one-element domain and degree zero. It follows that \(d\ge 1\) implies \(k\ge 2\), as required in Lemma 4.6.

Let _N_ be a positive integer and index the _N<sup>d</sup>_ bits of INDEX<sub>_N<sup>d</sup>_</sub> by the vectors \(u=(u_1,\dots,u_d)\in[N]^d\). For each \(i\in[d]\), create a group of variables \(X_i=\{x_{i,p}:p\in[N]\}\). The variable _x<sub>i,u<sub>i</sub></sub>_ will occupy coordinate _i_ of the constraint associated with _u_.

We also need variables for the coordinates in \[_k_\]\\\[_d_\]. These coordinates must receive the basepoint 0 in Bob’s assignments. Using one variable in every constraint would give that variable degree _N<sup>d</sup>_, which is too large for Lemma 4.6. We instead create variables _w<sub>j,p</sub>_ for every \(j\in[k]\backslash[d]\) and \(p\in[N]\), and use _w_<sub>_j,u_<sub>1</sub></sub> in coordinate _j_ of the constraint associated with _u_.

Formally, for \(u\in[N]^d\), define \(C_u=R(v_1^u,\dots,v_k^u)\) by setting \(v_i^u=x_{i,u_i}\) for \(i\in[d]\) and \(v_j^u=w_{j,u_1}\) for \(j\in[k]\backslash[d]\).

Alice receives \(b\in\{0,1\}^{[N]^d}\) and streams _C<sub>u</sub>_ exactly when _b<sub>u</sub>_=1. Let _P<sub>b</sub>_ be the resulting instance. It uses at most _kN=O<sub>R</sub>(N_) variables and at most _N<sup>d</sup>_ constraints. Every variable belongs to at most _N_<sup>_d_-1</sup> of the constraints _C<sub>u</sub>_. Fixing the index of that variable fixes at least one coordinate of _u_. The constraints have distinct ordered scopes because the variables from the groups _X_<sub>1</sub>_,...,X<sub>d</sub>_ determine _u_. They also have distinct unordered scopes. Indeed, the groups _X_<sub>1</sub>_,...,X<sub>d</sub>_ are disjoint. If _C<sub>u</sub>_ and \(C_{u^\prime}\) had the same unordered scope, then for every \(i\in[d]\) they would contain the same variable from _X<sub>i</sub>_. This would give \(x_{i,u_i}=x_{i,u_i^\prime}\), and hence \(u_i=u'_i\), for every _i_. Therefore \(u=u'\). This last fact is relevant when _R_ is symmetric.

Bob receives \(q=(q_1,\dots,q_d)\in[N]^d\) and wants to recover _b<sub>q</sub>_. His goal is to make _C<sub>q</sub>_ see all 2_<sup>d</sup>_ tuples from Lemma 7.4. At the same time, every constraint _C<sub>u</sub>_ with \(u\neq q\) should miss at least one of the _d_ choices, so that its positive and negative contributions cancel. To achieve this, Bob changes only the variable _x<sub>i,q<sub>i</sub></sub>_ in each group _X<sub>i</sub>_ and leaves every other variable at the basepoint.

For each \(S\subseteq[d]\), Bob considers the following assignment. In group _X<sub>i</sub>_, the variable indexed by _q<sub>i</sub>_ receives _a<sub>i</sub>_ if \(i\in S\), and all other variables receive 0. Every variable _w<sub>j,p</sub>_ also receives 0. In symbols,

\(\alpha^S(x_{i,p})=\left\{\begin{array}{ c c }
a_i, & \text{if}i\in S\text{and}p=q_i, \\
0, & \text{otherwise},
\end{array}\right.\alpha^S(w_{j,p})=0.\)

Consider first the queried constraint _C<sub>q</sub>_. In coordinate \(i\in[d]\), it receives _a<sub>i</sub>_ when \(i\in S\) and 0 otherwise, while every coordinate in \[_k_\]\\\[_d_\] receives 0. Thus, as _S_ ranges over all subsets of \[_d_\], this constraint sees exactly the 2_<sup>d</sup>_ tuples from Lemma 7.4, and its signed contribution is _c_.

Now consider _C<sub>u</sub>_ for \(u\neq q\). Choose _i_ for which \(u_i\neq q_i\). The variable _x<sub>i,u<sub>i</sub></sub>_ always receives 0, whether or not _i_ belongs to _S_. Hence the satisfaction of _C<sub>u</sub>_ is unchanged when we replace _S_ by \(S\triangle\{i\}\). These two sets have opposite signs, so the contribution of _C<sub>u</sub>_ cancels. We have proved that<tbc>

\(\sum_{S\subseteq[d]}(-1)^{d-|S|}\mathbf{1}[C_u\text{is satisfied by}\alpha^S]=\left\{\begin{array}{ c c }
c, & \text{if}u=q, \\
0, & \text{if}u\neq q.
\end{array}\right.\)

<tbc>Summing this identity over the constraints that Alice streamed gives<tbc>

\(\sum_{S\subseteq[d]}(-1)^{d-|S|}\mathrm{val}_{P_b}(\alpha^S)=cb_q.\)

<tbc>This identity determines _b<sub>q</sub>_ from the 2_<sup>d</sup>_ numbers \(\mathrm{val}_{P_b}(\alpha^S)\) because \(c\neq 0\). The difficulty is that an Exact-CSP algorithm returns an optimum, not the value of a chosen assignment. By Lemma 4.6, Bob can append constraints that hard-pin a complete assignment and make the optimum reveal any one of these values. More precisely, for each \(S\subseteq[d]\), Lemma 4.6 gives an instance \(H_{\alpha^S}\) satisfying<tbc>

\(\mathrm{OPT}_\mathrm{max}(P_b\cup H_{\alpha^S})=|H_{\alpha^S}|+\mathrm{val}_{P_b}(\alpha^S).\)

<tbc>By the final part of Lemma 4.6, Bob can construct \(H_{\alpha^S}\) from the public variable set, the assignment \(\alpha^S\), and the bounds _N<sup>d</sup>_ and _N_<sup>_d_-1</sup>. He does not need to know Alice’s string. The gadget uses _O<sub>R</sub>(N_) new variables, and \(P_b\cup H_{\alpha^S}\) is simple. When _R_ is symmetric, it has no repeated unordered scope.

Suppose now that the streaming algorithm uses _s(n_) bits of space. We first reduce its error so that each output is wrong with probability at most \(1/(10\cdot 2^d)\). This requires only _O<sub>R</sub>_(1) independent copies because _d_ depends only on _R_. Alice runs the amplified algorithm on _P<sub>b</sub>_ and sends its memory state to Bob. For each \(S\subseteq[d]\), Bob starts from a copy of this state, appends \(H_{\alpha^S}\), and obtains \(\mathrm{OPT}_\mathrm{max}(P_b\cup H_{\alpha^S})\). Subtracting the known number \(|H_{\alpha^S}|\) gives \(\mathrm{val}_{P_b}(\alpha^S)\). A union bound shows that all 2_<sup>d</sup>_ values are correct simultaneously with constant probability, after which Bob recovers _b<sub>q</sub>_ from the signed sum above.

There is a constant _A<sub>R</sub>_ such that every final instance uses at most _A<sub>R</sub>N_ variables. For any sufficiently large target value _n_, choose \(N=\lfloor n/A_R\rfloor\) and add unused variables so that the final instance has exactly _n_ variables. Then \(N=\Theta_R(n)\). We have obtained a randomized public-coin one-way protocol for INDEX_<sub>N<sup>d</sup></sub>_ with _O<sub>R</sub>(s(n_)) communication. By Lemma 3.7, \(s(n)=\Omega_R(N^d)=\Omega_R(n^d)\).

We have proved the required lower bound when _R_ is a core. It remains only to combine this with the reduction to the core and the upper bound proved above.

_Proof of Theorem 7.1._ Let _R<sup>⋆</sup>_=core(_R_). By Lemma 4.2, solving Exact-CSP(_R_) has the same streaming space complexity as solving Exact-CSP(_R<sup>⋆</sup>_). The deterministic upper bound follows from Lemma 7.2. If _d_=0, the indicator of _R<sup>⋆</sup>_ is constant, so _R<sup>⋆</sup>_ is either empty or equal to _C<sup>k</sup>_. This gives the last statement of the theorem. Suppose now that \(d\ge 1\). The randomized lower bound follows by applying Theorem 7.3 to _R<sup>⋆</sup>_. The reduction to the core preserves simple instances. If _R_ is symmetric, then _R<sup>⋆</sup>_ is symmetric and the reduction also preserves the unordered scopes. This proves all three parts of the theorem.

Thus the streaming complexity of Exact-CSP(_R_) on simple instances is governed, up to the logarithmic factor in the upper bound, by the degree of the core relation.

## 8 Conclusion and Open Questions

In this paper, we demonstrated that the core of a relation is vital for characterizing the streaming complexity of many optimization problems related to constraint satisfaction problems. We hope that this work encourages further exploration of the relationship between CSP cores and streaming complexity. We conclude with a handful of open questions.

• Can the algorithms presented in Theorem 5.1 and Theorem 6.1 be made efficient in terms of both space and time complexity? A key challenge in this regard is that there is no general technique for efficiently detecting if a CSP instance is non-redundant. If one could find such an algorithm, it would be a major milestone in the development of algorithms for CSP kernelization. See [CJP20; LW20; Car22; BG25] for further discussion.<tbc>

• In addition, our paper only considers _insertion-only_ streams. What if we allow both insertions and deletions?<tbc>

## A Literals and Non-Constant-Satisfiable CSPs

In this section, we show how our general CSPs core characterization recovers the two earlier results of Sharma and Velusamy [SV26a]. We first consider CSPs with literals and show that passing their shift/sign-closed language to the core does not change non-redundancy. We then show that a positive Boolean constraint language is a core exactly when it is not constant-satisfiable.

A _constraint language_ \(\Gamma\) is a fixed finite set of relations over the same domain. A map on the domain is an endomorphism of \(\Gamma\) if it preserves every relation in \(\Gamma\), and \(\Gamma\) is a core if every such endomorphism is an automorphism. As for one relation, we obtain core(\(\Gamma\)) by choosing an endomorphism \(\rho\) with minimum image and restricting every relation to that image.

Without loss of generality, we claim that the core reduction and the satisfiability arguments also work for a fixed finite constraint language. In the core reduction, each arriving _S_-constraint, for \(S\in\Gamma\), is replaced by the \(\rho(S)\)-constraint on the same scope. The satisfiability hard-pinning construction may similarly use constraints from any relation in \(\Gamma\). We will use this extension below without further comment.

### A.1 Literal CSPs as a special case

We first show that our general CSPs core characterization recovers the previous characterization for CSPs with literals. In the literal model, the domain is _D_=Z_<sub>q</sub>_, and every constraint may apply an arbitrary additive shift to each coordinate. For any relation \(S\subseteq D^\ell\) and any \(\lambda\in D^\ell\), write \(S^\lambda(x):=S(x+\lambda)\). Thus, for a relation \(R\subseteq D^k\), its _shift closure_ is<tbc>

\(\Gamma_R^\mathrm{lit}:=\{R^\lambda:\lambda\in D^k\}.\)

Then a CSP with literals over _R_ is exactly a positive CSP over \(\Gamma_R^\mathrm{lit}\). We write \(\mathsf{NRD}_n^+(\Gamma)\) for the largest number of constraints in a nonredundant positive \(\Gamma\)-instance on _n_ variables. Similarly, \(\mathsf{NRD}_n^\mathrm{lit}(R)\) denotes non-redundancy in the literal model over _R_.

For a constraint language \(\Gamma\), let \(\mathsf{SAT}(\Gamma)\) denote satisfiability for positive \(\Gamma\)-instances. The following corollary records the language version of our satisfiability characterization.

**Corollary A.1** (Satisfiability for constraint languages)**.** _For every fixed finite constraint language_ \(\Gamma\),

\(\Omega_\Gamma\big(\mathsf{NRD}_n^+(\mathrm{core}(\Gamma))\big)\le\mathsf{SPACE}(\mathsf{SAT}(\Gamma))\le O_\Gamma\big((\mathsf{NRD}_n^+(\mathrm{core}(\Gamma))+1)\mathrm{log}(n+1)\big).\)

_The upper bound is deterministic, and the lower bound holds for randomized bounded-error one-pass algorithms._

_Proof._ The core reduction replaces each relation in \(\Gamma\) by its restriction to the core domain and preserves satisfiability and streaming space exactly, as in Lemma 4.2. For a core language, the upper bound maintains a nonredundant subinstance with the same satisfying assignments, exactly as in Lemma 5.2. If the language contains a nonempty proper relation, disjoint constraints from this relation show that its non-redundancy is \(\Omega_\Gamma(n)\), so the space needed to try assignments is within the stated bound. Otherwise every relation is empty or full, and satisfiability can be decided by checking whether an empty-relation constraint appears. For the lower bound, the hard-pinning construction and the INDEX reduction in Theorem 5.3 work with constraints from any relation in the core language. This proves the two bounds.

The following lemma shows that passing to the core does not change non-redundancy for any shift-closed language.

**Lemma A.2.** _Let_ \(\Gamma\) _be a finite constraint language over D_=Z_<sub>q</sub> that is closed under coordinatewise shifts. Then_ \(\mathsf{NRD}_n^+(\Gamma)=\mathsf{NRD}_n^+(\mathrm{core}(\Gamma))\).

_Proof._ First, we may assume that every relation in \(\Gamma\) is nonempty. Empty relations are fixed by every shift and every endomorphism. Moreover, if a nonredundant instance contains an empty-relation constraint, then it can contain no other constraint. Empty relations therefore give the same trivial size-one instances before and after passing to the core, so we may discard them. If no relations remain, the statement is immediate.

For a relation _S_ and a coordinate _i_, let _S+de<sub>i</sub>_ denote the relation obtained by adding _d_ to coordinate _i_, where _e<sub>i</sub>_ is the _i_th unit vector. Define

\(H:=\{d\in D:S+de_i=S\text{for every}S\in\Gamma\text{and every coordinate}i\}.\)

Thus _H_ is the subgroup of shifts that are invisible to every relation.

Choose one representative from each coset of _H_, let \(C\subseteq D\) be the set of representatives, and let \(\rho:D\rightarrow C\) map every element to the representative of its coset. Since \(\rho(a)-a\in H\), for every \(S\in\Gamma\) and every tuple _x_,

\(x\in S\Longleftrightarrow\rho(x)\in S.\) (A.3)

In particular, \(\rho\) is an endomorphism.

We claim that \(\rho\) is a core endomorphism. Let \(h:D\rightarrow D\) be any endomorphism and write \(\delta(a):=h(a)-a\). We show that

\(\delta(a)-\delta(b)\in H\text{for all}a,b\in D.\) (A.4)

Indeed, fix \(S\in\Gamma\), \(x\in S\), and an arbitrary tuple _z_. Write \(\delta(z)\) for the tuple obtained by applying \(\delta\) to every coordinate of _z_. Since \(\Gamma\) is shift-closed, \(S^{x-z}\in\Gamma\), and \(z\in S^{x-z}\). Applying _h_ gives \(h(z)\in S^{x-z}\), or equivalently \(x+\delta(z)\in S\). Thus translation by \(\delta(z)\) maps _S_ into itself. Since translation is a bijection and _S_ is finite, it preserves _S_. Comparing two tuples \(z,z'\) that differ only in coordinate _i_, taking the values _a_ and _b_ there, shows that translation by \((\delta(a)-\delta(b))e_i\) preserves _S_. Since _S_ and _i_ were arbitrary, (A.4) follows.

Now suppose that _h(a_)=_h(b_). Then \(b-a=\delta(a)-\delta(b)\in H\). Hence an endomorphism cannot identify elements from distinct _H_-cosets. Every endomorphism therefore has image size at least |_D/H_|, while \(\rho\) has exactly this image size. Thus \(\rho\) is a core endomorphism.

Let \(\Delta:=\rho(\Gamma)=\mathrm{core}(\Gamma)\). For \(S\in\Gamma\), write \(S^\rho:=\rho(S)\). By (A.3),

\(x\in S\Longleftrightarrow\rho(x)\in S^\rho.\) (A.5)

Moreover, the map \(S\mapsto S^\rho\) is injective. If \(S^\rho=T^\rho\), then (A.5) implies _S=T_.

Now take any positive \(\Gamma\)-instance _I_, and replace every relation _S_ by \(S^\rho\), obtaining a \(\Delta\)-instance \(I^\rho\). This correspondence preserves the number of constraints. Moreover, (A.5) shows that an assignment and its image under \(\rho\) have the same satisfaction pattern, constraint by constraint. Consequently, if _a_ is a witness for a constraint in _I_, then \(\rho(a)\) is a witness for the corresponding constraint in \(I^\rho\). Hence \(I^\rho\) is nonredundant whenever _I_ is nonredundant.

Conversely, every \(\Delta\)-instance can be lifted to a \(\Gamma\)-instance using the unique preimage of each relation, and every witness assignment over _C_ remains a witness after this lift. Thus nonredundant instances of the same size exist in both directions, proving \(\mathsf{NRD}_n^+(\Gamma)=\mathsf{NRD}_n^+(\Delta)\).

Applying the lemma to the shift closure gives the desired connection to the literal model.

**Corollary A.6.** _For every_ \(R\subseteq\mathbb{Z}_q^k\), \(\mathsf{NRD}_n^\mathrm{lit}(R)=\mathsf{NRD}_n^+\big(\mathrm{core}(\Gamma_R^\mathrm{lit})\big)\)_. Hence our general core characterization recovers the previous streaming characterization for_ CSPs _with literals._

_Proof._ A literal _R_-instance is exactly a positive \(\Gamma_R^\mathrm{lit}\)-instance, so \(\mathsf{NRD}_n^\mathrm{lit}(R)=\mathsf{NRD}_n^+(\Gamma_R^\mathrm{lit})\). Since \(\Gamma_R^\mathrm{lit}\) is shift-closed, Lemma A.2 gives \(\mathsf{NRD}_n^+(\Gamma_R^\mathrm{lit})=\mathsf{NRD}_n^+\big(\mathrm{core}(\Gamma_R^\mathrm{lit})\big)\). Together with Corollary A.1, this recovers the one-pass satisfiability characterization for CSPs with literals.

## A.2 Non-constant-satisfiable Boolean CSPs

We next recover the previous characterization for positive Boolean CSPs. A Boolean constraint language \(\Gamma\) is _constant-satisfiable_ if there is a value \(c\in\{0,1\}\) such that the constant tuple (_c,...,c_) belongs to every relation in \(\Gamma\). Equivalently, assigning the value _c_ to every variable satisfies every positive instance over \(\Gamma\). The next lemma shows that excluding this case is exactly the same as requiring the language to be a core.

**Lemma A.7.** _Let_ \(\Gamma\) _be a Boolean constraint language in which every relation is nonempty. Then_ \(\Gamma\) _is a core if and only if it is not constant-satisfiable._

_Proof._ Every non-bijective map from {0,1} to itself is constant. The constant map with value _c_ is an endomorphism of \(\Gamma\) exactly when (_c,...,c_) belongs to every relation in \(\Gamma\). One direction is immediate. For the other, apply the constant map to any tuple in each nonempty relation. Thus \(\Gamma\) has a non-bijective endomorphism exactly when it is constant-satisfiable.

It follows that every non-constant-satisfiable Boolean constraint language is already a core. Applying our general CSP core characterization therefore directly recovers the positive Boolean result of Sharma and Velusamy.
